item.title: Old Bitly links are being hijacked
item.description:
Update, 15 November, 23:40 UTC: CNN reports redirected Bitly links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense as well. Our third check of the Trump links, at 23:35 UTC, found nothing new: 49 links re-created years after their tweets still work.

Update, 15 November, 22:30 UTC: Bitly has confirmed the problem. In a post on X at 19:13 UTC it said it had identified an issue that “allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links” and send people to unrelated content. Bitly said it has suspended the accounts involved and is disabling the affected links. It added that its Trust and Safety team is working on protections against similar misuse.

Update, 15 November, 19:30 UTC: The Burger King and McDonald’s links no longer redirect. Both were still working at 15:05 UTC and returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page by 19:22 UTC. The same has happened to the two extra Trump links we verified and to six of the seven links in our sample that pointed somewhere new. The seventh now shows a Bitly warning that the account that created it has been suspended. The 49 re-created links that look like the originals still work.

Burger King’s X account was not hacked. A Bitly short link in a tweet the chain posted on 24 July 2011 was registered again by someone else on 15 November 2026 and pointed at Wikipedia’s list of Nazi concentration camps. The tweet was advertising a restaurant locator. A post quoting it passed 2 million views within hours, and Burger King’s original has since become unavailable.

It was not the only one. Eighteen minutes earlier a Bitly link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011 was registered the same way and pointed at Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Ransomnews also checked 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009 to 2013, taken from a public archive. Bitly’s own link pages show that 56 were created after the tweets they sit in, and a 57th is blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam. Four were registered on 15 November. Two more, created in January 2024 and January 2025, point at domains that copy the names of crypto services.

In brief Burger King posted the tweet on 24 July 2011 with the short link bit[.]ly/19BFiM. Bitly’s information page for that link gives a creation time of 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 and a destination on Wikipedia. A link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011, bit[.]ly/mLWJO0, was created again at 05:14 UTC the same morning, 18 minutes before Burger King’s. It opens Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Both tweets have since become unavailable. Nobody posted from either company’s account. The links changed hands on Bitly’s side, so the old tweets send readers wherever the new owners choose. Of 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009 to 2013, 40 are still the original. Another 49 were created again later but lead where the tweets suggest, 48 of them in a 17-minute run on 26 May 2023. Seven lead somewhere else and one is blocked by Bitly. Four of those seven were registered on 15 November 2026 between 07:49 and 09:57 UTC. They open a Roblox profile, a YouTube video (twice) and a Wikipedia article about Trump and Jeffrey Epstein. One Trump tweet from April 2011 carries three links to videos of his children. All three have been replaced. Bitly’s help pages say the ending of a bit.ly link cannot be reused, even after the account behind it is deleted. In February 2025 it was reported to have fixed a bug that allowed this. We found no public statement from Bitly, Burger King or McDonald’s by 14:30 UTC on 15 November. By 19:22 UTC both links returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. None of the seven Trump links that pointed somewhere new redirects any more. Bitly confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC. It said it has suspended the accounts involved and is disabling the affected links. CNN reported the same evening that old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense were affected too. We have not checked those links ourselves. Was Burger King hacked?

No. Nothing was posted from Burger King’s account and nothing suggests anyone got into it. The tweet is 15 years old and reads as it always did, pointing followers to “our handy restaurant locator” through a Bitly link. What changed is where that link goes. As with the Microsoft 365 outage three days earlier, the first question people asked was whether it was an attack on the company, and the answer is the same.

Bitly keeps a public information page for every short link. Add a plus sign to the end of the address and it shows where the link points and when it was created. For bit[.]ly/19BFiM that page gives the destination as Wikipedia’s “List of Nazi concentration camps” and the creation time as 15 November 2026, 05:32 UTC. A link printed in a tweet from 2011 can only carry a 2026 creation date if the same ending was issued a second time.

We tested the method on links nobody disputes. A link whose creator says he made it in 2009 shows a 2009 creation date. A custom link tweeted by a YouTube channel on 21 June 2017 shows 20 June 2017. Among the Trump links that are still original, 32 of 40 were created on the day of the tweet or the day before.

The post that spread it came from an X user at 06:51 UTC, 79 minutes after the link was created, and had 2.2 million views by early afternoon.

By 13:45 UTC the Burger King post inside it was showing as unavailable. We do not know whether Burger King removed it or X did. The short link was still redirecting to Wikipedia at 13:47 UTC.

Was McDonald’s hacked?

No. Its link was changed 18 minutes before Burger King’s. On 7 June 2011 McDonald’s tweeted a Bitly link to something its team in Sweden had done. Bitly’s information page for bit[.]ly/mLWJO0 shows the link was created at 05:14 UTC on 15 November 2026, and it redirects to Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. The tweet was returning a not-found error when we checked at 14:20 UTC.

The two changes are close in time and alike in style. The X user Alex Greenland, who spotted both timestamps, thinks one person or group is probably behind them. Nothing we have seen proves that.

How does an old Bitly link get hijacked?

Someone registers its ending again. The part of a Bitly link after the slash is called the back-half. Bitly generates one at random, or the user types a custom one. If an old link stops existing and its back-half can be claimed, whoever claims it decides where every tweet, email, PDF and printed QR code carrying that link now leads. No password is stolen and no account is touched, so the brand that posted the link sees nothing wrong.

Bitly says this cannot happen. Its help page on deleted accounts states that bit.ly links keep working and that their back-halves “cannot be re-used”, whether they were generated or custom. A separate page says Bitly deletes accounts that have been inactive for three years. The creation dates we collected do not fit the first statement. Back-halves that appear in tweets from 2009 to 2012 belong to links created between 2023 and today.

It has happened before. In February 2025 Disruptionist reported that memecoin promoters had taken over Bitly links in 2013 posts by Donald Trump and Melania Trump and pointed them at token listings. According to that report, a bug let people claim a back-half once the original link or its account had been deleted or deactivated, and Bitly fixed it and switched off the hijacked links. Links created on 15 November 2026 show the same thing is possible now.

The X user Damin Toell identified it as link hijacking at 07:25 UTC and noted that old Trump posts were affected too.

At 09:18 UTC another user described the method in a post that has been viewed more than 46,000 times. Three more Trump links were registered in the 40 minutes that followed.

Free tool

How does your own site score?

Run the same forty passive checks against your own domain: TLS and certificates, security headers, SPF and DMARC, cookies before consent, and what your stack quietly reveals. A grade out of 100 in about fifteen seconds.

No signup. Nothing installed. We only request what your site already serves publicly.

How many old links have been replaced?

More than half of the ones we tested. We took every tweet Donald Trump’s account posted from 2009 to 2016 from the Trump Twitter Archive data set on GitHub, left out retweets and extracted the bit.ly links. That gave 97 different links, first used between 2009 and 2013, with 61 of them from 2011. We chose this account because its old posts were named in the reports of 15 November and in the 2025 case, and because a full public archive exists. For each link we recorded where it redirects and the creation date on Bitly’s information page, at about 13:45 UTC on 15 November 2026.

Forty links are untouched. Forty-nine were created again later and lead to addresses that fit the tweets: mostly videos on Trump’s YouTube channel, plus pages at CNBC, CNN and the Wall Street Journal. Forty-eight of those were created between 14:55 and 15:12 UTC on 26 May 2023, roughly one every 20 seconds. We do not know who did that. It looks like a repair job by someone who knew where each link used to go, and it means those back-halves were free to claim by May 2023.

That leaves eight links that now lead somewhere their tweets never pointed.

Tweet date What the tweet promoted Link created again Where it goes now 3 Jun 2009 An iGoogle page 15 Nov 2026, 07:49 UTC A Roblox user profile 1 Jul 2010 A golf course in Scotland 15 Nov 2026, 09:36 UTC A YouTube video 17 Sep 2010 A QVC jewellery show 15 Nov 2026, 09:47 UTC The same YouTube video 7 Oct 2010 A golf course in Scotland 15 Nov 2026, 09:57 UTC Wikipedia’s article on Trump and Jeffrey Epstein 14 Mar 2011 A video blog 29 Jan 2025, 21:09 UTC test[.]com 25 Apr 2011 A video of Donald Trump Jr. 18 Jan 2025, 21:43 UTC worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com 25 Apr 2011 A video of Eric Trump 17 Jan 2024, 11:08 UTC dappradars[.]website 25 Apr 2011 A video of Ivanka Trump Not shown Blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam
One tweet, three replaced links

On 25 April 2011 the account posted three Bitly links to “The Next Generation” videos of Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump and Eric Trump. The first now leads to worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com, a domain that borrows the name of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture. The third leads to dappradars[.]website, one letter away from the crypto analytics site DappRadar, at a path named “eligibility/check”. Bitly blocks the second with a notice that it was “flagged as redirecting to malicious or spam content”.

WHOIS records from WhoisXML API show both domains were registered afresh after the links were created. The current registration of dappradars[.]website began at 02:56 UTC on 15 November 2026, through Hostinger, although the Bitly link that points there was created in January 2024. The domain now forwards to a YouTube video. The current registration of worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com dates from 11 April 2026, through Namecheap, almost 15 months after the link was created, and its HTTPS certificate failed verification when we checked. We have not seen what either domain served when the links were first made.

A replaced link can be replaced again. When the domain behind it lapses, the next buyer inherits whatever traffic the old tweet still sends.

More Trump links outside our 97

X users found replaced Bitly links in Trump tweets from 2012 and 2013 that the archive stores only as t.co addresses. We checked two. The link in a tweet of 10 January 2013 was created at 23:52 UTC on 14 November 2026 and opens a page on Steam. The link in a tweet of 10 September 2012 was created at 01:04 UTC on 15 November and opens a YouTube video. Late on 14 November is the earliest change in this wave that we have seen.

Which re-created links still work?

We ran the same check on the 97 Trump links twice more, at 19:25 and 23:35 UTC on 15 November. The seven links that pointed somewhere new no longer redirect. The other 49 links created years after their tweets still do: 48 were made within 17 minutes of each other on 26 May 2023 and one in February 2025. They point to what look like the original pages, mostly YouTube videos and news articles. We do not know who re-created them or why. The 40 original links work as before.

How we counted

We used the archive’s condensed yearly files for 2009 to 2016 and found bit.ly links only in tweets up to 2013. From late 2011 Twitter wrapped links in its own t.co shortener, and the archive stores most later links in that form (1,218 of them in 2012), so Bitly links behind those are not among our 97. A link counts as created again when Bitly’s information page shows a creation date more than 30 days after the first tweet that used it. In practice the gap was at least 11 years in every case. Destinations were read from the redirect header without opening the pages. The count covers one account and one link shortener. It shows that these links were claimed. How many of Bitly’s older links can be claimed is something only Bitly can answer. Domain registration data is from WhoisXML API.

Who else was affected?

CNN reported on the evening of 15 November that old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense carried redirected Bitly links too, along with a 2013 post from McDonald’s Indonesia account. It counted at least a dozen in Trump’s posts, in a wave that appears limited to posts from 2009 to 2014. Burger King told CNN it had nothing to do with the redirects.

We have not checked those links ourselves. Bitly was already disabling affected links when they were reported, and a disabled link no longer shows when it was created. The accounts we verified directly are Burger King, McDonald’s and Donald Trump.

What happened on 15 November 2026?

The first change we found came late on 14 November. The McDonald’s and Burger King links followed at 05:14 and 05:32 UTC the next morning. All times below are UTC and on 15 November unless stated.

Saturday 14 November: the earliest change we found 23:52 Link takenA link in a 2013 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a page on Steam, the earliest change we found. Sunday 15 November, morning: the brand links are taken 01:04 Link takenA link in a 2012 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a YouTube video. 02:56 Domaindappradars[.]website, the target of a Trump link replaced in 2024, is registered afresh. 05:14 Link takenThe back-half in McDonald’s 2011 tweet is registered and pointed at Wikipedia. 05:32 Link takenThe back-half in Burger King’s 2011 tweet is registered and pointed at Wikipedia. 06:51 XAn X user quotes the Burger King tweet. The post goes on to pass 2 million views. 07:25 XAnother user identifies it as link hijacking and says old Trump posts are affected. 07:49 Link takenA link in a 2009 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a Roblox profile. 09:18 XA user describes the method in public. 09:36 to 09:57 Links takenThree links in 2010 Trump tweets are registered. Sunday 15 November, afternoon and evening: Bitly responds 13:45 Burger KingBurger King’s post shows as unavailable. Its link still redirects to Wikipedia. 14:20 McDonald’sMcDonald’s post returns a not-found error. Its link still redirects to Wikipedia too. 15:05 Our checkBoth links still redirect to Wikipedia. 19:13 BitlyBitly says on X that an issue let old, inactive links be repurposed, that it has suspended the accounts involved and that it is disabling the affected links.Why it matters: this is the first confirmation from Bitly that old links could be taken over. 19:22 Our checkBoth links return Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. So do six of the seven Trump links in our sample that pointed somewhere new and the two we verified outside it. The seventh shows a warning that the account that created it has been suspended. 21:10 CNNCNN reports redirected links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense. 23:35 Our checkOur third check finds no further change. Forty-nine re-created links in the Trump sample still redirect. Status NowThe Burger King and McDonald’s links no longer redirect, and neither do the Trump links that pointed somewhere new. Forty-nine re-created links in the Trump sample still work. Bitly has not said how many links were taken. Checked at 23:35 UTC on 15 November. Why does a joke link matter?

Because the same move works for fraud. The examples from 15 November are pranks: a Wikipedia page, a game profile, a video. The 2025 wave pushed memecoins, and two of the Trump links in our table lead to domains named after crypto services. A link inside an old post from a verified brand, a bank, a ministry or a news outlet carries that account’s credibility, and X shows the post exactly as it was written. Readers have no reason to doubt it.

The exposure is wider than X. The same short links sit in old emails, PDFs, slide decks, printed QR codes and help pages. Security researchers file this under broken link hijacking: a link outlives the thing it pointed to, and someone else moves in.

What should brands and readers do?

Any organisation that posted short links years ago should assume some of them are no longer its own.

List the short links in your old posts. Export your post archive from each platform and pull out every bit.ly address. Check each one. Add a plus sign to the link and compare Bitly’s creation date with the date of your post. A later date means the link is no longer yours. Remove what you cannot fix. Delete posts whose links were replaced or no longer resolve, and report replaced links to Bitly. Use a short domain you own for new links, so nobody else can issue the same address.

For everyone else, the checks take a few seconds.

Do not trust a link because the post is old or the account is verified. The account owner may have no control over where it goes. Preview before you click. Adding a plus sign to a bit.ly link shows the destination without visiting it. Be most careful with pages that ask you to sign in or connect a crypto wallet. What happens next?

Bitly has to say whether old back-halves can still be claimed and what it will do about the ones already taken. We found no public statement from Bitly, Burger King or McDonald’s by 14:30 UTC on 15 November. Later that day the links that pointed somewhere new were deactivated, and 49 others created years after their tweets were left working. Bitly confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC and said it was still disabling affected links. Its statement does not say how many links were taken or how. Checks like this one are what our breach verification desk is for, and we will update this article when either company responds or the numbers move.

Frequently asked questions Was Burger King hacked in November 2026?

No. Nothing was posted from Burger King’s X account. A Bitly short link in a tweet from 24 July 2011 was registered again by someone else on 15 November 2026, so the old tweet began sending readers to a different page.

Was McDonald’s hacked?

No. A Bitly link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011 was registered again at 05:14 UTC on 15 November 2026 and pointed at Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Nothing was posted from the McDonald’s account.

Why did a Burger King tweet link to a list of Nazi concentration camps?

The tweet’s Bitly link, bit[.]ly/19BFiM, originally advertised a restaurant locator. Bitly’s information page shows the link was created again at 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 with a Wikipedia article as its destination. Burger King did not choose that destination.

What is Bitly link hijacking?

It is when someone registers the ending of an old Bitly link that no longer exists and points it at a page of their choice. Every old post, email or document that carries the link then leads to the new destination. No account is broken into.

How can I tell whether a Bitly link has been replaced?

Add a plus sign to the end of the link. Bitly shows the destination and the date the link was created. If the creation date is later than the post or document the link appears in, the link is not the original.

Were Donald Trump’s old tweets hacked?

No. Ransomnews checked 97 Bitly links in tweets from 2009 to 2013. Fifty-six were created again after the tweets were posted and one is blocked by Bitly. Seven of them lead to destinations unrelated to the tweets, including two domains that copy the names of crypto services.

Has Bitly fixed the problem?

A fix was reported in February 2025 after links in Trump posts were pointed at memecoin pages. Links created on 15 November 2026 show that old endings can be claimed now. Bitly had made no public statement that we could find by 14:30 UTC that day. It confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC and said it was disabling the affected links. It added that its Trust and Safety team is working on protections against similar misuse.

Who else was affected by the Bitly link hijacking?

CNN reported redirected Bitly links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense, as well as Burger King, McDonald’s and Donald Trump. Ransomnews verified the Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump links directly.

Are the hijacked Bitly links still active?

The ones we tracked are not. By 19:22 UTC on 15 November 2026 the Burger King and McDonald’s links, and the Trump links that pointed somewhere new, returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. Bitly said it was still disabling affected links, so check any old short link before you trust it.

item.title: Preserving 30 years of Salon journalism
item.description:
When Salon launched in 1995, the web was still finding its voice. One of the first major publications born on the internet, Salon helped define a new kind of digital journalism, bringing together politics, culture, criticism, and ideas for a generation of online readers.

After 31 years, Salon has announced that it is ceasing publication. But thanks to web archiving, the stories don’t have to disappear.

The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has been preserving Salon for nearly three decades—the online publication has been published over time at salon1999.com, salonmag.com and, since 1999, salon.com. Today, more than 250,000 Salon articles can be discovered through the Wayback Machine, representing a record of digital journalism and the conversations that shaped our culture since the earliest days of the web.

To make exploring this web archive easier, we’ve also launched an experimental Salon Explorer, a new interface for discovering Salon’s archived journalism. Browse more than 250,000 articles and explore the work of over 20,000 writers using filters that make it easier to find stories and discover writing you may have missed.

item.title: What's Next for Nvidia?
item.description:
Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned 33 years after he co-founded the company.

What happens to a company when a visionary CEO is gone? Most often innovation dies and the company coasts for years on momentum and its brand. Rarely does it regain its former glory.

That’s the danger facing Nvidia. Here’s what their board should be considering.

Here’s why.

Jensen Huang reinvented Nvidia three times. In 2006 he launched CUDA, turning a graphics chip for PC gamers into a general-purpose computing platform – and funded it for years ahead of any revenue. In 2012, when researchers used Nvidia chips to win the ImageNet contest, he pointed the company to deep learning. In 2020, with the acquisition of Mellanox, Nvidia went from selling boards with GPUs to selling integrated racks that power AI datacenters.

These were not just product transitions, but radical business model transitions; new channels, new customers and new markets. Nvidia pivoted from a vendor of graphics boards, to a software platform, and then to systems company. It’s hard to imagine a CEO focused on executing an existing business model funding CUDA through those years.

Steve Jobs did the same at Apple, transforming it from a niche computer company into the most profitable company in the world. Between 2001 and 2008, Jobs reinvented the company three times.

Visionary CEOs are not “just” great at assuring world-class execution of a successful business model, they are also world-class innovators.

The best are agile and know how to pivot, making substantive changes to their business model while or before their market has shifted. The very best of them shape markets – they know how to create new markets by seeing opportunities before anyone else. They remain entrepreneurs.

Visionary CEOs don’t need someone else to demo the company’s key products for them. They deeply understand products, and they have their own coherent and consistent vision of where the industry/business models and customers are today, and where they need to take the company. They know who their customers are because they spend time talking to them. They use strategy committees and the exec staff for advice, but none of these CEOs pivot by committee.

Microsoft and Apple are two examples of what happens when a visionary CEO is replaced by an execution CEO.

Microsoft and the Cost of Missing the Next Market Microsoft entered the 21st century as the dominant software provider for anyone who interacted with a computing device. After running Microsoft for 25 years, Bill Gates handed the reins of Microsoft to Steve Ballmer in January 2000. Ballmer went on to run Microsoft for the next 14 years.

Ballmer organized the company around execution of its then current strengths – Windows and Office businesses. He tripled Microsoft’s sales to $78 billion and profits more than doubled from $9 billion to $22 billion, but those results hid missed opportunities that would reshape computing.

Ballmer failed to understand and execute on the five most important technology trends of the 21st century: in search – losing to Google; in smartphones – losing to Apple; in mobile operating systems – losing to Google/Apple; in media – losing to Apple/Netflix; and in the cloud – losing to Amazon.

In early 2014, Satya Nadella took charge. Nadella got Microsoft organized around the cloud (Azure), freed the Office and Azure teams from Windows and killed the phone business. Nadella saved Microsoft from irrelevance. Today Microsoft is worth about $4 trillion. It is one of the few companies that regained its former glory, after its board replaced a salesman with a product and engineering insider.

Innovation CEOs Hire Execution VPs Successful visionary CEOs build an executive staff of world-class operating executives and technical leaders (and they unconsciously force out any world-class innovators from their direct reports). The problem is in a company driven by a visionary CEO; there is only one visionary.

Nvidia is the extreme case. Jensen had about 60 direct reports and discouraged one-on-one meetings. No long-term plans. Much like Jobs, he made himself the point where technical, product and business decisions came together. Replacing that role is harder than filling a box on an organization chart. He said he didn’t believe in succession planning.

When visionary founders depart (resignation, death, firing, etc.), their operating executives believe it’s their turn to run the company. At Microsoft, Bill Gates chose Steve Ballmer, and at Apple Steve Jobs chose Tim Cook. Jensen anointed no one.

Once in charge, one of the first things these operations/execution CEOs do is to get rid of the chaos and turbulence in the organization. Execution CEOs value stability, process and repeatable execution. On one hand that’s great for predictability, but it often starts a creative death spiral – creative people start to leave, and other executors (without the innovation talent of the old leader) are put into more senior roles – hiring more process people, which in turn forces out the remaining creative talent. This culture shift ripples down from the top and what once felt like a company on a mission to change the world now feels like another job.

(Amazon is a counterexample. Before succeeding Jeff Bezos, Andy Jassy had already founded and led AWS. He was an innovator who had built a new business inside the existing company.)

At Nvidia this step isn’t optional. No one else can run a company with 60 direct reports, so the next CEO’s first move will be to add layers of management.

Why Tim Cook Was the New Steve Ballmer Tim Cook ran Apple for 15 years. Apple under Cook grew its revenues from $108 billion to $416 billion and its market value from $350 billion to about $4 trillion. The iPhone continued its annual upgrades of incremental improvements. The transition to Apple silicon showed that major technical change on the chip level was possible under his leadership. But Apple silicon was a better engine for the existing products Apple already had, not a new market.

Apple stumbled badly on the one major product category launched under Cook – Apple Vision Pro and missed badly on AI (Siri was actually first with a Chatbot.) This year it turned to Google to help fix Siri. In September 2026 Cook handed the job to John Ternus.

How Nvidia Could Miss the Boat The threat to Nvidia is already visible: its biggest customers are becoming its competitors. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Tesla are all building their own AI chips. Jensen’s answer was to keep innovating and bring to market a new generation of chips every year, build a moat around an integrated hardware and software platform (CUDA), and invest ~$50 billion in the AI labs that run on Nvidia.

It’s likely these are the bets an execution CEO trims first.

The irony is that in the 21st century, the tighter you hold on to your current product/markets, the likelier you will be disrupted. The rapid change of technology will create new disruptions that will force “bet the company” decisions about product direction, markets, pricing, supply chain, operations and the reorganization necessary to execute a new business model. In the GPU market, the difference between market dominance and Chapter 11 may be a hands-on product/customer, and business model-centric CEO with an entrepreneurial vision of the future.

Four Challenges for the Board of Directors The dilemma facing the board at Nvidia or any board of directors on the departure of an innovative CEO is strategic: Do we still want to be an innovative, risk taking company? Or should we now focus on execution of our core business, reduce our risky bets and maximize shareholder return. Ultimately a board would like both – preserving the speed and ambition of Jensen’s decision-making while distributing enough authority for the company to function without him.

Tactically, that question results in asking: Do you search for another innovator from outside, promote one of the executors or go deeper down the organization to find an innovator?

Herein lies four challenges.

Steve Jobs and Bill Gates chose execution executives as their successors. The result was they confused world-class execution with the passion for product and customers, and market insight. From the perspective of Gates there was no difference between him and Ballmer and Jobs believed Cook could be equally creative. Yet history has shown they were world-class stewards of a business model each had been handed. Yet long-term survival in markets that change rapidly require innovation and execution.. Nvidia’s board has a different version of this problem. Jensen suggested no one, and he left the board the day he left the job. The decision belongs to a board in crisis, led by the first chair the company has ever had. Boards in crisis reach for stability. That gets you an execution CEO by a different road. Nvidia’s board should ask what its candidates have built under uncertainty. If the board decides that the company needs another innovator at the helm, you can almost guarantee that the best executor – the number 2 and/or 3 vice president in the company – will leave, feeling that they deserved the job. Now the board is faced with not only having lost its CEO, but potentially the best of the executive staff. Many innovative/visionary CEOs have become part of the company’s brand. Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Jensen Huang. This isn’t a new phenomenon, think of 20th-century icons like Walt Disney, Edwin Land at Polaroid and Henry Ford. But they’re not only an external face to the company, they were often the touchstone for internal decision-making. Years after a visionary CEO is gone, companies are still asking, “What would Walt Disney/Steve Jobs/Henry Ford have done?” rather than figuring out what they should now be doing in the changing market.Jensen was more than the brand. He set Nvidia’s foreign policy, and was the company’s face in Washington, Beijing and Taipei. No Nvidia operating VP has done that job. The next Nvidia CEO inherits a Congress and investigators asking how many restricted Nvidia chips reached China. As companies grow larger and management falls prey to the fallacy that it only exists to maximize shareholder short-term return on investment, companies become risk averse. Large companies and their boards live in fear of losing what they spent years gaining (customers, market share, revenue, profits.) This may work in stable markets and technologies. But today very few of those remain. And certainly not Nvidia’s market.

Lessons Learned

Nvidia’s order book and CUDA will make the next two or three years look fine no matter who is CEO (unless a meaningful share of that revenue turns out to be chips that were diverted to China.) Innovation CEOs are almost always replaced by one of their execution VPs If they have inherited a powerful business model (like Nvidia) this often results in gains in revenue and profits that can continue for yearsHowever, as soon as the market, business model, technology shifts, these execution CEOs are ill-equipped to deal with the changeThe result is a company obsoleted by more agile competitors and their company is left to live off momentum in its twilight years Nvidia’s board has to decide what it is hiring its next CEO to do. Executing today’s business is essential. So is reinventing it before someone else makes it obsolete. Execution pays your salary, innovation pays your pension

item.title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker
item.description:
Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details.

GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC.

The issue

uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page.

The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html. That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters.

Basically the attack here is:

Figure out the element picker URL Create our own invisible (opacity 0) iframe that embeds it Drive the picker to put the filter we want in it Position the invisible iframe to trick the user into pressing the invisible “Create” button Figuring out the element picker URL

On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation.

On the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch. From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension://<extension UUID>/web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn’t do anything.

But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID.

const origOpen = XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open; XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open = function(m, url, ...a) { const e = /^moz-extension:\/\/[^/]+/.exec(url); if (e) { e[0] // <- has the extension UUID! } return origOpen.call(this, m, url, ...a); };

Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it’s not just this one filter rule.

Creating an iframe

Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html`.

Sending messages to it

Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message1 to enable the create button and set opt.

Normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn’t let you add scriptlet filters. But there’s a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There’s an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image. But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script.2

This is where the main issue is - the element picker shouldn’t accept messages from the attacker. One of the fixes was having a secret password that the real element picker gets from the content script, that the element picker sends in the initial postMessage.

Getting the click

I didn’t bother actually implementing this, but malicious websites could overlay stuff on top of the embedded element picker or make it invisible by setting the iframe opacity to 0. So as long as the website can get the user to click on the page, it can add arbitrary trusted filters for arbitrary domains.

Filters added by the element picker are always treated as trusted (at least until a recompile), which is why it can add a trusted filter. If the user later changes their custom filters it would cause a recompile, clearing the filter trust. But in practice the attacker could just immediately open the victim webpage, so this doesn’t help much.

item.title: Interpreting claims that a theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean
item.description:
This post is an attempt to explain in simple terms how to interpret claims of the form “this theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean”. The summary is: there is an important signal that can be extracted from Lean code, but if this code is AI-generated then you need to do some tests first. We explain the tests, and note that in many cases (such as the OpenAI theorem dump) these tests have not yet been systematically done.

Introduction

Last month’s theorem dump by OpenAI consisted of 722 mathematics papers, around 45% of which came with some Lean code. Three of the (non-Leanified) papers have since been retracted because of a sign error. Some people might say “well, the papers that come with Lean code are definitely correct because that’s how Lean works”. Others might say “well Lean had a soundness bug and could well have more, and AIs will reward hack, so Lean verification doesn’t tell us much at all”. The truth, unsurprisingly, is more subtle, and this post is an attempt to explain it.

This post is structured as a sequence of four questions that one needs to ask about a Lean repository, particularly if it is AI-generated, before one can start to make correctness claims of this form. And before I start, let me stress that for many of the papers in the OpenAI theorem dump, these questions have not yet all been answered affirmatively (but there is nothing stopping people from answering these questions, and I have no reason to believe that any of the tests below will fail, it’s just that people didn’t do them yet).

Question 1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement?

A Lean repository will typically have a “headline theorem statement”. This will be some computer code which defines the statement (not the proof!) of a theorem. Note the huge difference here between the statement, and the proof. For example here is some fully-compiling Lean code which defines a mathematical statement.

import Mathlibdef FermatsLastTheorem : Prop := ∀ a b c n : ℕ, n ≥ 3 → a^n + b^n ≠ c^n

This code imports Lean’s mathematics library Mathlib and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean ℕ contains 0, so a = b = c = 0 and n = 3 gives a counterexample. This does not stop the statement from compiling! It will however stop any proof of this statement from compiling. Lean carefully distinguishes between the statement of a theorem and the proof of a theorem; humans are very good at referring to both ideas as “a theorem”.

The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem.

Things are, however, not always as easy as this. Currently, because of deficiencies in available libraries, one may have to read many thousands of lines of code just to understand the statement of a formalised theorem. An example of this right now is a PR to DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository containing a Lean formalisation of the statement of the Hodge conjecture. At the time of writing, the statement relies on over 10,000 lines of code sitting on top of Mathlib, because Mathlib (which is carefully human-expert-checked and which can be trusted) does not yet have the definitions of things like the cycle class map needed to make the statement. Another example is Axiom’s recent announcement of a formally-verified proof of the classification of finite simple groups. The statement which Axiom’s system proved is here in Tau Ceti, an AI-generated library of Lean code. The file containing the statement imports over 250K lines of Lean code in Tau Ceti (over 900 files). Of these, around 5600 lines of code are crucial because they contain all the relevant definitions (for example, all the definitions of the sporadic simple groups, most of which are still not in Mathlib). Without human checking, one does not really know for sure that this is definitely the correct statement of the classification (and note that I have not yet met any human who claims to have carefully checked that the definitions of the sporadic groups in Tau Ceti are correct). In fact by far the strongest evidence that we have that this statement is correctly formalized is that Axiom’s code proves it!

It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper. And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had. To give a concrete example: paper 194 claims to prove Lech’s multiplicity conjecture in commutative algebra, with no restriction on dimension, residue field or characteristic; this question has been open since 1960. The headline theorem in the corresponding Lean code can be checked to be Corollary 5.4 of the paper — already an impressive achievement, but not the headline result.

Question 2: does the code compile?

Once you’re convinced that you understand the statement of the theorem which the Lean code purports to prove, you (or perhaps one of your friends who has access to a beefy machine, if the code base is huge) has to actually compile the code.

When Anthropic formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean, they asked me to take a look at the 13 million lines of code which they had generated. I downloaded it onto my machine, dumped it into a sandbox (because who knows what AI-generated code will do, it can in theory delete all your files) and attempted to compile it; I very quickly ran out of memory. I told Anthropic that I was unable to make any claims about what they had done until I could see the code base compiling, and they gave me temporary access to a machine with 96 cores and 500 gigs of ram. I could then compile the code.

Of course, with a more reasonably-sized codebase it is possible to compile the code on a reasonably-sized machine. For example OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier-Stokes problem is 640K lines of code and compiles fine on my laptop.

It is probably worth stressing again: do not run random Lean code on your local machine unless you sandbox it first. Lean’s mathematics library is safe to run and build upon because this is human-curated and checked by human experts. AI-generated code is not.

Question 3: does the code prove the theorem as stated?

I already talked in Question 1 about the importance of checking the statement of a theorem, so we can be sure that the code is proving the right thing. However, there is an added complication here. Ideally the statement of a theorem will be contained in a file which has very few imports beyond Mathlib, so we know we can trust it. But the proof of the theorem will necessarily import thousands and possibly millions of lines of code which nobody wants to read. How do we know for sure that there is no trick hidden in the millions of lines of proof files which redefines x^n to mean 37, and then proves that a^n + b^n ≠ c^n because the left hand side is 37+37=74 and the right hand side is 37? Or which adds a new axiom to mathematics saying that the theorem is true? Put another way — given a Challenge.lean file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a Solution.lean file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which looks identical, how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics,

The one-line answer: lake comparator. You can read more about this answer here. But in short, this tool checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved via untrusted imports are identical, and that only the axioms of mathematics are used in the proof.

Question 4: does the code exploit a bug in Lean’s official kernel?

This can happen. There was a soundness bug in Lean’s kernel which was fixed four hours after it was discovered, and a subsequent review of Lean’s code base by OpenAI found several more, all of which were fixed before they were announced publicly. There may in theory be more soundness bugs in Lean’s kernel. However, this does not matter.

Why not? Because Lean now has many kernels, created by users, written in many different languages, and at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level. If you want to make absolutely sure that there is no reward-hacking then again there is a one-line answer: lake comparator --paranoid. A malicious piece of code exploiting an as-yet-undiscovered bug in Lean’s official kernel will not pass this test unless it exploits as-yet-undiscovered bugs in many independent systems all at once. For example this webpage from the Lean kernel arena demonstrates that OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier–Stokes problem is accepted by multiple kernels as well as Lean’s official kernel.

One final remark

Even if the Lean code compiles and passes all these tests, and is thus overwhelmingly likely to be a correct proof of a theorem, this does not mean that any corresponding pdf also contains a correct proof! The Navier–Stokes lost in translation paper demonstrates the opposite in fact, for the Navier-Stokes write-up; whilst all the tests above have been run for the Navier–Stokes work, there are instances where the pdf proof and the Lean proof diverge. In these cases, who knows if the pdf proof is OK! My understanding is that some experts have been using AI to informalise the Lean proof back into English in order to read the argument, rather than ploughing through the slop in the pdf.

Summary/conclusions

“It’s true because it’s checked in Lean” can be made to make sense. But one has to do some work beyond “the Lean code compiles”. Your frontier AI model can do all of this work. But it needs to be done, and (depending on the amount of Lean code in the proof) it may be computationally costly.

item.title: Winudf – DVD / BluRay driver for DOS, Windows 1.x – 3x / 95 / 98 / ME
item.description:
WINUDF reads and writes UDF (versions 1.02 to 2.60), the file system of DVDs, Blu-ray discs, packet-written CDs and UDF-formatted USB sticks and disks: WINUDF.EXE gives DOS and Windows 1.0x–3.11 drive letters for them, WINUDF.VXD is a file system driver for Windows 95 / 98 / ME with long names.

WINUDF is one of the four WINDRV packages, each in its own repository and usable alone or together with the others:

Package What it drives WINDISK IDE, SATA AHCI and NVMe disks, IDE/AHCI CD/DVD drives, SD card readers and eMMC WINUSB USB host controllers and devices, PS/2 mouse and keyboard, touchpads, USB4 / Thunderbolt WINAUDIO HD Audio, AC'97 and the Intel audio DSP (SST / SOF), General MIDI synthesizer, Sound Blaster 16 emulation for DOS programs WINUDF the UDF file system (DVD, Blu-ray, packet-written CDs, UDF disks), read and write
System WINUDF MS-DOS 3.10 – 8.0, FreeDOS UDF volumes (WINUDF.EXE) Windows 1.0x, 2.x (real mode) UDF volumes (WINUDF.EXE) Windows/386 2.x not tried Windows 3.0, 3.1, WfW 3.11 UDF volumes as network drives (WINUDF.EXE) Windows 95 / 98 / ME UDF with long names (WINUDF.VXD, IFS Manager file system driver) (§3)

From DOS (or an MS-DOS box of Windows 95 / 98 / ME), in bin\DOS of this package:

INSTUDF default directory, AUTOEXEC.BAT / SYSTEM.INI updated INSTUDF C:\DRV /O /L:R another directory; options for WINUDF.EXE after /O (letters from R:)

DOS / Windows 3.x: WINUDF.EXE goes to AUTOEXEC.BAT after MSCDEX, LASTDRIVE=Z to CONFIG.SYS when needed. Windows 95 / 98 / ME: WINUDF.VXD goes to WINDOWS\SYSTEM and device=WINUDF.VXD to [386Enh] of SYSTEM.INI. The originals are saved as *.WNF. Uninstall: UNINUDF.

DOS and Windows 1.0x–3.11: LASTDRIVE=Z in CONFIG.SYS, and in AUTOEXEC.BAT after the MSCDEX line: C:\WINDRV\WINUDF.EXE Windows 95 / 98 / ME: copy bin\WIN9X\WINUDF.VXD to C:\WINDOWS\SYSTEM and add device=WINUDF.VXD to the [386Enh] section of SYSTEM.INI. bin/DOS DOS: the driver, its 32-bit core, tools, installer and uninstaller (also all Windows 1.0x / 2.x need) bin/WIN3X Windows 3.0, 3.1 and Windows for Workgroups 3.11 bin/WIN9X Windows 95, 98 and ME (Plug and Play drivers and their INF files: the folder to give to "Have Disk" / "Update Driver") src the source code (see "Building")

Files used by several systems are in each of their folders. The installer is run from bin\DOS; it takes the files of the other systems from the folders next to it, so the bin tree has to stay together (copy all of it to a floppy or a directory).

Folder Files bin/DOS INSTUDF.EXE, MANUAL.TXT, README.TXT, UNINUDF.EXE, WINUDF.EXE bin/WIN3X WINGRP.EXE, WINUDF.TXT bin/WIN9X WINGRP.EXE, WINUDF.TXT, WINUDF.VXD

MANUAL.md (MANUAL.TXT in bin\DOS, WINUDF.TXT for Windows) describes everything else: all options, how the driver works, hardware and chipset notes, the programming interface, building from source, tests and known limitations.

1.2 (2 November 2026)

Changelog:

Program Manager (Windows 3.x): an Uninstall WINUDF item with a red cross on the disk icon (Windows closes, UNINUDF /REBOOT runs and restarts the computer). The banner lists the systems (DOS, Windows 1.x/2.x/3.x/95/98/ME). Windows 95/98/ME: programs on UDF discs (and WINUDF's own installer) no longer crash with 0xC0000005. The buffer of a read or write is locked before the driver starts: a page of the program's own image could be paged in from the same disc in the middle of the request, and the page-in then used the driver's block cache and transfer buffer, so the program got the data of the page-in. Extents of files written or filled are never longer than an extent can describe (just under 1 GB): a hole filled at once was one extent of any size (and its length overflowed into the type bits); merging blocks into the last extent can no longer overflow either. DOS: buffers are normalized before device transfers, so a 32 KB transfer never runs past the end of a 64 KB segment. Long file names: INT 21h 716Ch passes the caller's mode, attributes and action to DOS as they are (the create action was masked off); on DOS 3.x, which has no function 6Ch, the file is opened with function 3Dh (issues #9, #12). INT 21h 7142h accepts negative positions, like DOS's own seek (issue #11). The high dword of a file position beyond 4 GB is kept in the file's system file table entry (offset 07h, free for a redirector) instead of a table of eight entries: any number of open files can be beyond 4 GB (issue #10). Before staying resident, handles 0-19 are closed without looking at the job file table (issue #8). Unloading follows interrupt handlers whose IISP header has a jump of any kind before the 'KB' signature (issue #7). The texts of WINUDF.EXE, the VxD and the documentation name Windows 1.0 to ME.

1.1 (26 October 2026)

Changelog:

Added long file names in DOS: WINUDF.EXE answers the long file name API of MS-DOS 7 (INT 21h AX=71xxh: find first / next, open / create, attributes, rename, delete, directories, short / long name, file times), so DIR, COPY and other programs of MS-DOS 7.x show and use the long names of UDF disks; free space (7303h) and 64-bit file positions (7142h) for files of 4 GB and more. WINUDF.EXE is a regular DOS program that can be loaded high (LH), about 70 KB resident; its interrupt handlers follow the IBM interrupt sharing protocol, so it unloads (/U) after other TSRs that hooked the same interrupts. Works next to SHSUCDX (UDF DVDs of SHSUCDX's drives) and MSCDEX. Fixed unloading and the "already loaded" check. Fixed Windows 98 freezing on UDF disks in partitions Windows 9x calls unformatted (they are read through the BIOS path now). Fixed the "disk structure is corrupted" error when copying folders to UDF disks in Windows 98. Fixed WritePrivateProfileString (INI files) and Explorer writing desktop.ini hanging on UDF drives in Windows 95/98/ME: WINUDF.VXD answers the drive IOCTLs (removable, remote, drive map) itself. Added writing to Windows 10 UDF 2.60 disks (metadata bitmap embedded in its file entry). The volume is written and closed when the disk is removed safely. Added MS-DOS 7.0, 7.1, 8.0 and FreeDOS support; the installer puts WINUDF.EXE into AUTOEXEC.BAT there too (only Windows 95/98/ME use DOSSTART.BAT). The documentation is split into README.md (overview, installation) and MANUAL.md (all details).

1.0 (12 October 2026) — first release: UDF 1.02–2.60 read / write, WINUDF.EXE for DOS and Windows 1.0x–3.11, WINUDF.VXD for Windows 95 / 98 / ME.

1.0 update (14 October 2026): the package is split into bin/DOS, bin/WIN3X and bin/WIN9X; English documentation.

The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life

Two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore.

Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well.

So I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever.

I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he said “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.”

And so it is.

So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick.

Forget up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A. This little code is now the coolest “cheat” code I know…

1st off this works on any laptop/model not just think-pad. This isn’t a magic trick, the point of this besides the static discharge, this resets the Bios of computer by pulling all the charge out of the Internal 2032 CMOS Battery, which in return reboots the BIOS. This can happen for many reason not just a static charge, Some computers can have a bad infection that activates when the computer goes to sleep mode, this is a well known attacker, then the virus proceeds to overload your machine to shut down thus causing the bios to have the command programmed to stay shut down. Well by doing the manual BIOS RESET such as this, resets the configurations in the bios back to default.

Also you can try pulling battery out, unplugging charger, and then hold power button for 1 minute if the 10X an 30sec hold doesn’t work for you. And if for some reason it still don’t work, removing the 2032 CMOS Battery on the MOBO for 1 minute or replace it, the battery which is usually located near the RAM on most laptops, not all have the battery located in same place, I suggest if you need to go that far google your model of computer to locate the internal CMOS Battery.

I hope this helps

item.title: Many of Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday “deals” offered no savings
item.description:
Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive

A blockbuster new investigation from Groundwork Collaborative exposes how Amazon shoppers may be getting hosed during the retail giant’s much-touted Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events. The report, Deal or Decoy? Amazon’s Deceptive Discounts, examines products the retailer showcased as some the “best” discounts of the year to shoppers hunting for bargains during these sale events. A closer look at hundreds of these “deals” finds that Amazon frequently offered shoppers the same price, or in some cases a higher price, during recent holiday sale events than they could have paid just weeks earlier.

The report’s authors, Breyon Williams, Elizabeth Pancotti, and Lindsay Owens, find that nearly 1 in 3 of these Amazon “deals” offered no real savings – the exact same products were sold for the same price or less in the month before the sale. During Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales in the past two years, prices for nearly 1 in 10 products advertised as “deals” were higher than what customers could have paid for the products in the month leading up to the sales.

Groundwork’s analysis examined the prices of more than 350 products included on Amazon’s own deal pages for the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events in 2024 and 2025. These pages promote these deals as some of the “best” deals available. Amazon’s Black Friday 2025 deals page says, “With so many deals to explore, we’ve handpicked some of the best ones you’ll find.”

Groundwork Collaborative President and CEO and report co-author Lindsay Owens, shared the following reaction:

“Millions of Americans wait all year for Black Friday and Cyber Monday to score the biggest bargains on stocking stuffers and household staples. Shoppers trust that the deals advertised to them deliver real savings because Amazon promotes them that way. But it turns out that these major sales aren’t all they’re cracked up to be. Instead, our investigation reveals that shoppers who wait for these major sale events may be playing rip-off roulette.

“Amazon dominates online shopping, and families count on its sale events to stretch their dollars. With the holiday shopping season upon us and prices continuing to rise, shoppers deserve to know they can trust every deal Amazon promises them. If Amazon can’t deliver that basic promise, lawmakers should hold them accountable.”

Owens is the author of the recent book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet, which exposes how corporations are sophisticated pricing schemes to overcharge consumers.

The report’s key findings include: The price of nearly 1 in 3 products that Amazon described as “deals” was the same – or higher – during sale events than what customers could have purchased them for in the month leading up to the sale.Some Amazon “deals” offered shoppers higher prices than they could have paid before the sale. On Black Friday 2025, a pair of yellow Hunter Women’s Short Rain Boots “on sale” for $126.99 had been $79.97 nine days before the sale event started, meaning customers looking for a deal could’ve paid 59% more if they waited for the sale.On Cyber Monday 2025, a pair of men’s UGG Butte boots “on sale” for $179.98 had been $98.40 roughly four weeks before the start of the sale event, meaning the “deal” cost 83% more than the recent low.Among these “worse” deals, the median sale-event price was 19% higher than what shoppers could have paid for the products in the weeks leading up to the sale. Since learning of our study, Amazon has removed the aforementioned deal pages our study drew from, but archived versions of these pages can be found at the following links: Black Friday 2024, Cyber Monday 2024, Black Friday 2025, Cyber Monday 2025. Amidst the ongoing affordability crisis, millions of Americans count on holiday sale events, like Black Friday, to deliver real savings. In 2025, a record 203 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, and this year, 70% of U.S. customers plan to take advantage of holiday promotions. Deal or Decoy calls on federal and state regulators to crack down on misleading discounts and require retailers to show the lowest price a product sold for in the previous 30 days when advertising a sale.

ADDITIONAL BACKGROUND

The new report builds on Groundwork’s work exposing corporate pricing abuses and delivering results for American consumers.

In December 2025, Groundwork teamed up with Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union to expose how Instacart was charging shoppers different prices for the exact same groceries at the same store and time. Following the publication of Groundwork’s Owens’ book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet, the Federal Trade Commission launched an investigation into major retailers’ use of customers’ personal data to set prices, adding to growing scrutiny of corporate pricing practices and their impact on Americans’ wallets in response to Groundwork and Owens’ research. In October 2026, Groundwork exposed Walmart’s creepy patent filings and pricing playbook. The report digs into patent filings, privacy disclosures, and technology investments to reveal how the retailer is building the infrastructure that could allow it to deploy personalized pricing at scale.
