item.title: The Active Directory Era Is Finally Over
item.description:
The Active Directory Era Is Finally Over

“Life was simpler on Active Directory, at least I could manage every identity”.

I made that quote up, but there is nostalgia for a golden age of corporate IT that’s never coming back: Many enterprises still (try to) track identities in Active Directory (AD), a service that’s old enough to drink and crumbles at the scale of modern cloud computing.

It held up because the architecture is simple enough: Active Directory is an LDAP directory to store identities and a Kerberos implementation to let them authenticate, wrapped in decent UX and with continued updates.

AD accomplished the goal of identity management: A way to know all identities, who vouched for them, and where they’re valid. It answered three questions in a unified catalog:

What identities exist? With the directory, which records every user and machine What vouched for the identity? With a domain controller that approves authentication based on admin credentials Where is the identity valid? With AD domain architecture that reflects the company’s infrastructure

Security policies are moot if you can't answer any one of them. I spent many hours keeping our Active Directory catalog accurate so it could answer these questions, because everything downstream depended on it: issuing certificates automatically with Certificate Services, applying settings at scale with Group Policies, and more.

There were always some compromises: databases with local users, Linux servers requiring workarounds (Thank you SSSD!), but most users and machines in my network had an identity in Active Directory, and I knew which didn’t.

But unifying every identity in Active Directory (or any one directory) is nearly impossible with modern cloud architecture. There’s an AD ecosystem of security products, password rotations, and sync plugins that modernizes it, but nothing can undo architecture choices from a bygone era.

Active Directory is the new mainframe: great for its time, but you’d never choose to start from scratch. Replacing it is impossible because it’s so entrenched.

Active Directory can accurately reflect human identities with a few integrations and plugins, but machine identities are nearly impossible.

Maybe that’s controversial. You can come to me with torches, pitchforks, and architectural diagrams about Kubernetes pod identity attestation in AD, but Active Directory is still a piece of infrastructure built for a bygone era.

Visibility and attestation: Unified machine identity is nearly impossible in Active Directory

Most organizations are creating grave security risks because they don’t understand modern machine identity. I once spoke to someone at a conference who told me they had recently discovered a publicly exposed Lambda function. Bad enough, but that function’s policy was iam:* meaning it could take any IAM action, including crowning any attacker the organization’s superadmin. Oh, and by the way, this was a defense organization.

If an organization with high security requirements makes these blunders, you don’t want to know what happens at other organizations. This problem isn’t specific to AD, but it is a symptom of organizations not figuring out how to correctly attest machine identity in modern software development.

To understand why no organization can account for all of its machine identities in AD, we need to understand how a machine enters a domain. A domain is an administrative boundary that shares security rules. In practice, this is usually an organization.

When a new machine joins your domain, three main events happen:

An object is created inside the directory (often called a machine account) DNS is updated, certificates are issued (assuming you have AD Certificate Services autoenrollment) Kerberos tickets are issued so the machine can assert its identity

When that machine logs in, it authenticates to a Domain Controller (the server running Active Directory for the domain), which trusts it because the machine is in its directory. But the machine had to enter the directory first.

When Active Directory was built, that meant a human manually added it. “Machines” were physical servers that got delivered to the office, installed in the server dungeon room, and registered by a human admin.

Human approval doesn’t scale to developers creating and deprecating testing databases, Kubernetes clusters, and CI runners at will. Contemporary AD implementations deal with this by deferring authority. An admin token (sometimes hardcoded…) automatically joins new identities.

Using human credentials to join new machines is a workaround that negates the point: Admin approval implies a human can tell you about each trusted device.

No admin can know every EC2 instance, PostgreSQL database, or CI runner in the organization. This is also because when AD was built, machine identities were long-lived devices, not ephemeral cloud resources.

Active Directory was built for human approval of long-lived infrastructure, but now often auto-approves short-lived cloud resources.

Even if you built all of the complex automations to reflect every testing database and Kubernetes pod in AD with automated admin approval, it’s security theater. The unified directory would exist on paper, but lack authority.

Modern cloud infrastructure automatically asserts machine identity:

In Kubernetes, each pod gets a service account token, which allows it to assert its identity within the cluster. In Azure, you can configure a machine identity in Entra ID and let Azure’s Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) automatically issue OAuth tokens when machines request them.

These two examples have modern assumptions baked in: machines need to self-serve their identities when they’re spun up. They also assume a narrow scope.

Scope: how identity perimeters have changed

The unified directory of identity management aimed to encompass every device, user, and piece of infrastructure. Authenticating to the Domain Controller would be enough to get access to everything a user/machine needs and nothing they don’t.

This is the identity perimeter: where an identity is valid. In the Active Directory era, the perimeter was as large as possible. The more complete the perimeter, the more authoritative the directory. As an example, SQL Server accepts Windows authentication (i.e. an AD identity) or SQL authentication (username and password). Active Directory admins choose Windows auth to keep the perimeter large.

Anything outside of the directory would be a “shadow identity”: a valid identity that grants access to corporate infrastructure, but isn’t accounted for in identity management (unless you consider the post-it note on my monitor identity management).

A separate username-password set creates a separate perimeter. This used to be a problem, but is now the norm. Each API key, database string, or auth token creates a separate perimeter because they’re a credential that represents an identity for just one service. As an example, GitHub automation requires personal access tokens or GitHub private keys and doesn’t work with any directory identity.

But just to make it harder, zero-trust architecture makes machines constantly authenticate to each other, which skyrockets the count of credentials and creates hundreds of perimeters.

In theory, a small perimeter shrinks the blast radius of any breach: A compromised Notion session token should only give Notion access. In practice, an attacker may find additional credentials in Notion, which lets them expand their access. Oh, and the physical security layer of firewalls and physical perimeters is gone in the cloud era, so a leaked credential works from any attacker’s laptop.

This should concern admins more than it does: many teams keep troves of sensitive plaintext credentials in .env files or hardcode them in configuration files. The response is often lackluster:

Use SSO where it’s available for human users Teach the team how to securely handle plaintext machine credentials

A solution like Active Directory is nearly useless for solving these issues.

The new paradigm

Organizations can tame the complexity of machine identity in the cloud, but not as simply as one massive Active Directory list. Instead, we see two main vectors to fix this:

The first is identity federation, where one platform trusts another platform’s approval to authenticate a workload. All three major clouds support this.

Using OpenID Connect (OIDC), AWS can sign a token for an EC2 instance to access PostgreSQL in Azure. Entra federated credentials natively support this use case and would trust the EC2 workload.

This works for many use cases. If you’re exclusively on AWS and run Terraform from GitHub Actions, OIDC federation straight into IAM does the job: You get visibility, know why you trust it, and know its scope. But it’s laborious to implement each relationship, which means it relies on IAM administrators who can barely keep up with group membership requests. Moreover, if said pipeline is breached by, say, a supply chain attack (which are common nowadays), the whole perimeter is breached.

Even if your admins are bored, no cloud has native bridges between every possible tool, so federation stops as soon as any service only accepts an API key. Organizations shouldn’t accept unruly, long-standing plaintext credentials outside of security purview.

That’s why organizations adopt a brokering approach. Here, credentials live in a secrets manager like Infisical (which securely stores and then delivers secrets to workloads at runtime). This creates a meta-perimeter for all of those micro-perimeters. Infisical (or another tool) acts like a broker: Machines authenticate to it, they broker access to the credential store, and inject the credentials the identity can read into its runtime.

These two patterns can bring order to the Wild West of machine identity in the cloud era. They check the boxes Active Directory once did:

What identities exist? You have an overview of who authenticates and what they do What vouched for the identity? You know where workloads originate and why they’re trusted without relying on a human to approve everything Where is the identity valid? Keys, tokens, and strings have a natural perimeter.

This is especially important as organizations increasingly adopt AI agents, which often need their own identities, separate security policies, and even separate security tooling. Getting machine identity right is more important than ever. If you can’t keep track of testing databases and a Stripe API key, you don’t want autonomous software that can create its own databases and send that API key to strangers online.

item.title: A 512 KiB binary message teaching chess without a shared language
item.description:
Golden Board

Or Why and How to Teach Chess to Aliens.

Intro

Golden Board is a binary message designed to teach chess to an unknown recipient without a shared language, culture, or prior knowledge of the game. It begins by teaching the format needed to read its own contents.

The full project code and documentation are available on GitHub.

This guide follows that process: recover numbers from the bits, use them to reconstruct pictures and interactions, then learn how those pictures describe chess. One complete game connects the layers, from its physical bits to its final displayed position.

Feedback is always welcome.

Before we dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things about the project.

What does it look like?

In a nutshell, Golden Board is a sequence of 4,194,304 bits, or 512 KiB of ones and zeros. That number suggests arranging them into a 2,048 × 2,048 square.

What’s inside?

The first 64 rows contain 32 drawings, each 64 × 64 cells. Together they form the bootstrap: it teaches how to read the rest of the message. It's chess-agnostic and can be used to decode other structured messages.

The payload below contains visual chess lessons, exercises with feedback, complete games, and the information needed to find, check and display them.

Where did the idea come from?

I took inspiration from messages intended for unknown intelligences, such as the Voyager Golden Record, Lincos, and others.

But instead of sharing scientific knowledge or works of art, Golden Board teaches chess.

Why chess?

Two reasons.

First, a small set of rules opens up an enormous world of possibilities, ideas and beauty.

Second, a game can share more than knowledge: it offers a glimpse of the human mind.

How did I test it?

I ran trials using LLMs as stand-ins for unknown recipients, testing decoding and understanding with raw bits, decoded content, and varying levels of assistance.

Correctly recovering the bytes and understanding the lessons are separate tests. These models already know chess, so correct chess answers alone cannot establish that the message taught them. The trials helped identify ambiguities and improve the design; they do not establish that an unknown intelligence would understand it. Read the trial account.

How did I choose the games?

No set of 64 games is complete.

I chose games for their chess: brilliant attacks, surprising sacrifices, clever defenses, quiet strategy, and beautiful endings. The PGN anthology contains 64 games, while the binary message omits names, dates, and events.

What is it all for?

There is a special joy in sharing something you love.

What could we share with a civilization that knows nothing about us? They might already know our science or lack the context for our art, but chess can be taught from scratch, revealing centuries of human imagination, mistakes, and brilliance.

Most likely, no one will ever receive this message. But even a small chance that someone might discover a position with a move like Bf5 makes the whole thing worth trying.

Can you build on it?

Yes. The chess-agnostic bootstrap, binary format and Python tools offer a starting point for teaching other subjects without a shared language or culture. Developers can adapt the system; researchers can use the trials to investigate what works, what fails and why. Source code and documentation.

How to read this guide

In the source drawings, each cell shows a bit: black represents 1 and white represents 0. Decoded pictures are reconstructed from the stored data, rather than cropped from the source square.

Colors, fine gray guides, and labels are added here to make the pictures easier to read. They are not part of the original message.

The intended recipient can infer these arrangements without visual aids, using bounding boxes, fixed sequence lengths, and other previously learned patterns.

The frame below provides an example; its contents are explained later. The blue area covers a data row and its small marks underneath. The orange area picks out the small number to its left. The green area covers a whole boxed list. The gray guides make individual bit positions easier to count.

Hover over a colored phrase to keep only its matching highlights. Hover over the picture to hide all visual aids.

Reading numbers and pictures

The recipient begins with a clean sequence of bits or a sampled square, and is assumed to be able to count, recognize patterns and write simple programs. Obtaining those cells from a signal or physical object is a separate problem.

The first task is to recover pictures and interactions from the bits. The recipient can then use those displays to learn chess. The bootstrap establishes the reading rules through worked examples; the recipient supplies a program that follows those rules. The message carries data for that program to interpret, not executable code.

The bootstrap is the narrow strip at the top of the view below. The payload area beneath it includes the unused space at the end.

Headers show order and related groups

Before looking inside each drawing, use its header to locate it in the strip. Each frame repeats the same corner mark. Its top row pairs a count of filled cells with a binary numeral to give its global number, 1–32. A second pair two rows below counts steps within a related group. That local count restarts for each group; standalone frames leave its row empty.

Compare these four headers. Frame 6 is sixth overall and second in its related group. Frame 3 stands alone:

Frame 1: global 1 (00000001), group step 1 (00000001).

Frame 2: global 2 (00000010), group step 2 (00000010).

Frame 3: global 3 (00000011), no local counter.

Frame 6: global 6 (00000110), group step 2 (00000010).

The corner crop below shows the same received pattern at four rotations:

As drawn

Quarter turn

Half turn

Three-quarter turn

The repeated corner suggests an orientation to try. Ascending counts, dimensions and checksums test whether it remains consistent. The corner alone does not prove orientation or which received state should represent 1.

Frame 1 of 32: Read numbers by counting

Binary numerals connect a pattern of bits to a quantity. This first frame makes that connection by pairing numbers with cells that can be counted.

The left-hand stripes contain 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and 15 filled cells. Opposite each stripe, the upper four-bit numerals give the same quantity: the empty stripe pairs with 0000, and two filled cells pair with 0010. The lower eight-bit numerals repeat the quantities with leading zeros.

Frame 2 of 32: Identify each bit position

A filled bit contributes a different amount depending on its position. Moving it one place left doubles that contribution. This frame pairs each single-bit pattern with its position number.

The left column starts with 00000001 and moves its single filled position one place left on each row, ending with 10000000. The right column counts those positions from 1 to 8, starting at the rightmost bit. Each horizontal pair belongs together.

Every field has a black border with a white inset around its data row. The border fixes the full width even when most positions are empty. The eight-bit patterns therefore stay in one column, while their four-bit position numbers stay in another.

Checking the recovered bytes

The recipient needs more than plausible-looking numbers before trusting the recovered lessons and games. A wrong orientation, bit interpretation or byte grouping can still produce values. Golden Board includes checks that let the recipient reject an inconsistent reading before using its content.

The content is organized into documents: collections of picture definitions, numerical data and display or interaction instructions. Each document’s bytes sit inside a checked block called a section. Its header identifies the document and gives its byte length. That length locates both the check at the end and the beginning of the next section.

A section also stores a checksum, a value calculated from its identifying fields and content. The program creating the message computes this value from the original bytes. The recipient repeats the calculation on the recovered bytes and compares the result with the stored check. A mismatch rejects that reading. A match supports the consistency of those bytes; it does not repair them or establish that their meaning has been understood.

Take section 2 from the actual payload. Its first six bytes form a header: the document’s number, called its ID, and the document’s byte length. The document itself follows, then the stored checksum. The calculation covers the header and every document byte, and stops before the stored check.

Golden Board uses CRC-32C for this calculation. The next drawings teach it with one input byte before applying the same method to a complete section. The immediate goal is to reproduce the sender’s check from the same bits.

Finding sections and documents

The recipient can now read numbers and reproduce a checksum. The next task is to find each section’s boundaries and recover the document inside it. The section is the checked storage wrapper; the document is the collection of things to display and use.

Those things are stored as records. Each record has a kind, a numeric name called an ID, and its own contents. For example, one record can define a small picture and another can refer to that picture by ID. Keeping the definition in one place lets many displays reuse it. IDs are assigned during message creation and stored in the data; the recipient reads them rather than inferring them from a shape. Their scope is one document.

An inventory lists the documents that must be recovered and the records where each may be opened. These starting records are its entries. They lead to a picture sequence or an interaction. An entry is a record’s ID, not its byte address.

To teach these relationships, the bootstrap contains a complete small worked document of 326 bytes. Its simple pictures and responses exercise the format before chess appears. Reading the five record types

Finding a document’s bytes does not yet tell the recipient how to draw its pictures or conduct its exercises. Its records divide that work into five kinds, all using the same named-record format.

A glyph stores a small rectangular bitmap. A display frame places glyph IDs in a larger grid, so the same bitmap can be reused in many cells. A trace starts from a frame and applies stored changes to indexed cells. This lets the message show a changing diagram or replay a game without storing every complete picture separately. When a game ends

A side with no legal move is checkmated if its king is in check, and stalemated otherwise. Checkmate is a loss; stalemate is a draw. Golden Board also recognizes three classes where neither side can give checkmate: king against king, king and bishop against king, and king and knight against king. Its rules machinery ends play after a legal move reaches one of these board endings, and refuses later moves or declarations.

A claim for threefold repetition becomes available once the current position has appeared at least three times. A fifty-move claim needs at least 100 plies since the last pawn move or capture. Neither condition ends play automatically: the side to move must explicitly claim the eligible draw. A move that would reach a threshold does not make that claim available in advance. The course shows eligible claims and the separate events that accept or refuse them.

Either side can resign while play is active, awarding the other side the win. Draw agreement requires both sides’ explicit consent after each has made a move. These declarations have known causes. An anthology score only records the outcome: a win or draw on a nonterminal board does not identify resignation, agreement or a claim.

This is the project’s practical chess profile. It excludes automatic fivefold and 75-move adjudication, intended-next-move claim procedures, tournament procedures, and a general solver for positions where checkmate is impossible. Material outside the three recognized dead-position classes receives no general deadness verdict.

Tactics, mating and strategic guidance

The later course builds on control and legality to teach attacks, defenses, pins and forks. A fork here is one piece geometrically attacking at least two opposing pieces. That fact alone does not prove that either capture is legal or profitable. A passed pawn has no opposing pawn ahead on its own or an adjacent file; it still faces kings, other pieces and the timing of play.

Mating instruction includes king-and-queen and king-and-rook continuations, with contrasts that end in stalemate. A legal line ending in mate can still depend on the opponent choosing a losing reply. To support a forced win, the winning side may choose its continuations, but every legal defensive move and every eligible defensive draw claim must be covered. All resulting branches must end in the asserted win.

The message carries finite worked examples of this distinction. One starts with White’s king on f3 and queen on h4, and Black’s lone king on g1. White moves the queen to g3. Black’s only legal moves are king g1→f1 and king g1→h1. The stored continuations answer the first with queen g3→f2 and the second with queen g3→g2; both give checkmate. Covering only one reply would leave the forced-win claim incomplete. The player presents these stored displays and tables without searching for a mating line.

Strategic lessons use observable facts such as development, central control, open files and mobility. Their rough material scale assigns 1 to a pawn, 3 to a knight or bishop, 5 to a rook and 9 to a queen; the king has no exchange value. These counts and comparisons provide guidance, not a verdict on the better position or best move. It then examines legal choices and the shown move’s effects, including captures, check and game endings. Comparisons remain limited to the continuations actually supplied.
