item.title: Nvidia was in trouble before the Jensen Huang mess
item.description:
Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

“Everything sold today was designed two-to-three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

China Challenge

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI, China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Trend Spotting

Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

item.title: Psychic: Like fzf but learns from your actions
item.description:
psychic: like fzf but learns from your actions psychic is a fast file browser with ML-powered ranking

Most days Iâm in the terminal cdâing into directories and opening files in my editor. In any given week itâs mostly the same files and dirs because Iâm working on the same projects. I was annoyed I had to remember where files live, and tired of tab-completing the same few paths. My computer should already know which file I want to open!

So I made psychic, a fast terminal-based file browser. It tracks the directories you go to and remembers which files you open. It trains a lightweight ML model on your data and ranks results using that model. It prioritizes interactivity and speed above all else: results update as you type and the UI renders in under 16ms.

Everything about how it works flows from a key design decision: it has to be fast enough to update within one frame after a keypress. Iâd rather do 10 fast searches in the space of a couple seconds, than 1 smart search that takes many seconds to complete.

I use psychic every time Iâm on my computer. Itâs become the main way I move around the filesystem. Some numbers: Since I started using it in October 2025,

Iâve opened it 1450 times. On average, I typed 1.6 characters before I had what I wanted. 29% of the time I typed nothing! psychic knew what I wanted, top result. All I did was open and hit enter. Median time from opening psychic to getting where I wanted to go was 2 seconds. 41% of searches happened within 1s, 69% within 3s. 80% of the time, I picked the top result. 96% of picks were in the top 3. The paths I selected were about 50 characters away, on average. So Iâm typing 3% of that to get there.

(These are from the built-in psychic stats command, which you can run on your own history!)

Itâs on homebrew: brew install kshitijl/tap/psychic.

On the left are search results. On the right is a preview of the file or directory currently selected. You type a query in the bottom and the results are filtered and ranked, changing with every letter. If you hit Enter on a file, it opens your terminal editor in the same window and waits in the background. If itâs a directory, it restarts the search from inside there. It remembers every file and dir you open, and a shell integration records every dir you cd into from outside psychic. All of those are included in every search.

Itâs like fzf and zoxide had a baby, plus a small ML model that learns your patterns and favorites. Itâs doing ad optimization on your own data, to help you navigate your computer faster.

How it works

All your searches and clicks get written to a sqlite db on your computer. psychic trains a LightGBM model on that data. The model learns to predict which files youâll open, based on your search query. psychic uses the model to rank search results. After every keypress, psychic reruns the model and reranks all results.

For more details, see the README in the repo.

Some key design decisions

The model I use is LightGBM, an implementation of gradient-boosted trees. Itâs tiny and fast and trains in seconds. It can learn rules that depend on threshold values. For example, it can learn a rule like âFiles above 1 MB are only opened if theyâve been modified in the last 24 hoursâ, like log files. LightGBM also has the excellent LambdaRank objective, which is specialized for exactly this kind of ranking task.

The latency budget ruled out any model thatâs not local: a network call could easily be over 10 ms or worse. It also ruled out LLMs or any kind of transformer model. Linear and logistic regression were too simple and performed much worse than LightGBM.

The model is re-trained from scratch every time you open psychic. This means it always reflects your current usage patterns. Training happens in the background and writes the model to disk when itâs done. We donât switch to using the new model while youâre looking at results, because itâs jarring when apps do that. Instead, we wait for when youâre not looking at the screen, like when youâre opening a file in an editor or when you click on a directory. Then we switch to the new model. Iâm proud of this careful little dance.

When a user has just started using psychic, there arenât enough clicks to train on. We use a simple model that rewards recent clicks, recent modification time and a fuzzy match between the query and filename. The final score is a weighted sum of the simple model and ML model. With few clicks, the simple model dominates. As more clicks accumulate, the ML modelâs score gets higher weight, until itâs basically 1.

How to be psychic

I use a carefully chosen set of features to try to predict which file youâll open. Some features are simple: how recently you last clicked it within psychic, its modification time, whether the filename starts with the query, a fuzzy text match score between the query and the filename. Hereâs a debug pane that shows the features and some performance stats:

One feature is ânumber of recent clicks on files that are in the same directory as this oneâ. This feature helps the model boost files that are in currently active projects.

The feature âclicks for this queryâ helps the model associate specific queries with specific files, without having to literally remember filenames and query texts. This way, while the model doesnât directly see filenames, it can still remember associations.

An episode is defined as everything that happens from opening psychic (or from the last click) to clicking on an item. So a single episode has a bunch of queries, including hitting backspace and trying new queries. The feature âengagements in episode with queryâ counts the number of times you clicked on a file at any point in an episode that had the current query. So if you always type âesâ and end up clicking on âbayesian-estimate.mdâ, then the model can see that association. Next time you type âesâ, the model will put that file at the top of the list.

Computer go fast

I watch perf closely and spent a lot of effort on a good benchmarking setup, plus perf logging. Every commit has performance benchmarks. If you use psychic and get bad performance, thatâs a bug! Let me know and Iâll fix it.

My tech choices were driven by performance. Probably the most important choices were Rust and LightGBM.

Syscalls are expensive but of course this whole program is syscalls. I tried to minimize syscalls. No filesystem syscalls in the main render loop; I carefully made sure that we ask for file metadata at the time we walk the filesystem and then carry that around everywhere else.

item.title: Jiff 1.0: A datetime library for Rust
item.description:
Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem.

Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”

This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.

Target audience: Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling.

Table of Contents The Jiff 1.0 Commitment

Jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd, Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0.

Unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my plan is to commit to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is important because the intent is for Jiff to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the ecosystem. They will not be made lightly.

To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please consult the CHANGELOG.

Introduction

In programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time. A human’s concept of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts.

A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime handling has historically been very difficult. My own belief is that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain. Instead of encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its users. Jiff instead tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to do something wrong. (Jiff is not the first to do this!)

In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions.

Follow Along

To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project with dependencies on jiff and anyhow:

mkdir jiff-playground cd jiff-playground cargo init --bin cargo add jiff anyhow $EDITOR src/main.rs

Most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code and replace whatever is in src/main.rs. Then run the program:

cargo run Terms

I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered with confusable terms, so I think it’s important to orient ourselves on a shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms, like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through exploration in the sections that follow.)

Civil time: The time you see on your clock. And in general, the time that the humans in your approximate geographic vicinity also see. That is, civil time is a human coordinated agreement for communicating time in a particular geographic region. Civil time is also known as: local time, plain time, naive time, clock time and others. UTC: An abbreviation for Coordinated Universal Time; it is a time standard that serves as the basis for civil time around the world. It was originally intended to roughly correspond to mean solar time. TAI: An abbreviation for International Atomic Time; it is a time standard as measured by atomic clocks. It isn’t directly connected to mean solar time. Leap second: An adjustment to TAI to bring it closer to mean solar time and thus forming the basis of UTC. Unix time: UTC, but ignoring leap seconds.

TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC.

The DateTime Onion

As a way to transition into some of the core types of Jiff, I’ve come to think of its datetime types like an onion. In reverse order, we can build up its layers all the way to a ZonedDateTime. So let’s start with more terms, but this time, they are also types in Jiff:

A civil::Date is a plain Gregorian date, unattached to any specific location. A civil::Time is a plain time on a clock, to nanosecond precision, unattached to any specific location. A civil::DateTime combines a civil::Date and a civil::Time to provide both a Gregorian date and a time on a clock. It is also unattached to any specific location. A Timestamp is an unambiguous specific instant in time regardless of geographic location, represented as the number of nanoseconds since the Unix epoch. A TimeZone is a set of rules for mapping a Timestamp to a civil::DateTime, and vice versa, in a specific geographic region. A ZonedDateTime combines a Timestamp, a civil::DateTime and a TimeZone to represent a specific instant in time in a specific geographic location.

To make this a bit more concrete, we can see what this looks like in code. Since a time zone can map from a civil datetime to an instant in time, one way to create a zoned datetime requires only a civil datetime and a time zone:

use jiff::civil; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let date = civil::date(2026, 11, 1); let time = civil::time(17, 30, 0, 0); let datetime = date.to_datetime(time); // zdt is an initialism for "ZonedDateTime" let zdt = datetime.in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!(zdt.timestamp().as_second(), 1793572200); Ok(()) }

Another way to create a zoned datetime requires only a timestamp and a time zone. This is because time zones can also map a timestamp to a particular civil datetime:

use jiff::{civil, Timestamp}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let timestamp = Timestamp::from_second(1793572200)?; let zdt = timestamp.in_tz("America/New_York")?; // This is a shortcut for creating a civil datetime. // The previous example spells it out a bit more verbosely // for clarity. let expected = civil::date(2026, 11, 1).at(17, 30, 0, 0); assert_eq!(zdt.datetime(), expected); Ok(()) }

Notice how we get the equivalent zoned datetime in both cases, but we come at it from different directions. In the first case, we start with a time that we might see on our clocks and calendars. In the second case, we start with a particular instant in time that we might get from a database or file system or some other system call.

Defining a time zone

There is one piece missing from the zoned datetime onion examples: the time zone offset. An offset represents the amount of time one must adjust UTC time in order to get civil time. For example, consider the time 2026-11-01T22:30:00 in UTC. In order to get the civil datetime for someone living in New York, one would subtract 5 hours:

2026-11-01T22:30:00 - 05:00 = 2026-11-01T17:30:00

Indeed, every zoned datetime has an offset associated with it:

use jiff::{civil, tz, Timestamp}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let timestamp = Timestamp::from_second(1793572200)?; let zdt = timestamp.in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset().seconds(), -(5 * 60 * 60)); let dt = civil::date(2026, 11, 1).at(17, 30, 0, 0); let zdt = dt.in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), tz::offset(-5)); Ok(()) }

NOTE: The America/New_York string you see in the above example is an IANA Time Zone Database Identifier. The IANA Time Zone Database is a collection of time zone definitions that can be referenced by a short identifier string. Examples: Australia/Sydney, Asia/Tokyo, Europe/Berlin.

When a civil datetime is combined with an offset, then what you get is always an instant in time.

With the concept of an offset introduced, we can now give a more precise definition of a time zone. A time zone is a geographic region in which civil clocks agree and which provides the following:

A mapping from an instant in time to an offset from UTC. The offset applied to an instant yields a civil datetime. A mapping from a civil datetime to a possibly ambiguous offset from UTC. The offset applied to a civil datetime yields an instant.

Both mappings have been demonstrated in prior examples, but the mapping from civil datetime to an offset seems to be rather complicated due to some potential ambiguity. When does that ambiguity arise? An ambiguous offset occurs when the civil datetime either doesn’t correspond to a valid clock time in this time zone (e.g., when clocks are moved ahead for daylight saving time) or where there could be multiple valid clock times (e.g., when clocks are moved backward for daylight saving time).

Let’s look at some examples. In this first example, we’ll take a look at times around the daylight saving time transition from summer time to standard time in New York. In New York, the clocks were “set back” by an hour at exactly 2AM. This caused the 1AM hour to repeat itself.

use jiff::{ civil::date, tz::{offset, TimeZone}, }; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let tz = TimeZone::get("America/New_York")?; // During summer time, New York's offset from UTC is -04:00. let zdt = date(2026, 11, 1).at(0, 30, 0, 0).to_zoned_datetime(tz.clone())?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4)); // During standard time, New York's offset from UTC is -05:00. let zdt = date(2026, 11, 1).at(2, 30, 0, 0).to_zoned_datetime(tz.clone())?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-5)); // But what does 01:30AM mean? Is it the first repetition or the second? // Jiff automatically chooses the first by default. let zdt = date(2026, 11, 1).at(1, 30, 0, 0).to_zoned_datetime(tz.clone())?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4)); Ok(()) }

The above example shows how Jiff resolves the ambiguity when a “fold” occurs, or when there is a time zone transition that moves the civil time backwards. But we can actually dig down into lower level APIs to change how that ambiguity is resolved. By default, Jiff uses a “compatible” strategy that always selects the first repetition of a time in a fold. But other strategies can be selected by using APIs on a TimeZone directly:

use jiff::{ civil::date, tz::{offset, TimeZone}, }; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let tz = TimeZone::get("America/New_York")?; let dt = date(2026, 11, 1).at(1, 30, 0, 0); // The same that Jiff uses by default. let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).compatible()?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4)); // Always selects the earlier datetime. // For a fold, this is the same as the // default "compatible" strategy. let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).earlier()?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4)); // Always selects the later datetime. // For a fold, this selects the second // occurrence of the 1AM hour! let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).later()?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-5)); // Always returns an error when there // is any ambiguity. assert_eq!( tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt) .unambiguous() .unwrap_err() .to_string(), "error converting datetime to instant in time zone America/New_York: \ datetime is ambiguous \ since it falls into a fold between offsets -04 and -05", ); Ok(()) }

The same idea applies to gaps, or time zone transitions where there’s some civil time that gets skipped on civil clocks. For example, on March 8, 2026 at 2AM, civil time skipped ahead to 3AM:

use jiff::{ civil::date, tz::{offset, TimeZone}, }; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let tz = TimeZone::get("America/New_York")?; let dt = date(2026, 3, 8).at(2, 30, 0, 0); // The "compatible" strategy selects // the later time in the case of gaps. let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).compatible()?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4)); // Always selects the earlier datetime. // For a gap, this selects the hour // before the gap. let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).earlier()?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-5)); // Always selects the later datetime. // For a gap, this is the same as the // default "compatible" strategy. let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).later()?; assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4)); // Always returns an error when there // is any ambiguity. assert_eq!( tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt) .unambiguous() .unwrap_err() .to_string(), "error converting datetime to instant in time zone America/New_York: \ datetime is ambiguous \ since it falls into a gap between offsets -05 and -04", ); Ok(()) } Durations

There are two remaining core types, both representing some notion of a duration:

Span is a powerful hybrid duration that combines both calendar units (years, months, weeks, days) and physical time units (hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds). It is a beefy type that preserves the individual unit values. SignedDuration is a signed version of std::time::Duration and always corresponds to a 96-bit integer number of nanoseconds. It can only represent physical time (units of hours or smaller) and not calendar units (units of days or greater).

A Span is the preferred duration type to use whenever possible. Here’s a simple example that shows how to get the number of days between two civil dates:

use jiff::civil::date; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let d1 = date(2024, 2, 1); let d2 = date(2024, 3, 1); let span = d2 - d1; assert_eq!(span.get_days(), 29); // or, equivalently: assert_eq!(d1.until(d2)?.get_days(), 29); // Flipping d1 and d2 gives the same result, // but negative. let span = d1 - d2; assert_eq!(span.get_days(), -29); Ok(()) }

Durations can also be added to dates:

use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let d1 = date(2024, 2, 1); // This convenient syntax comes from the // `ToSpan` extension trait. let span = 29.days(); assert_eq!(d1.checked_add(span)?, date(2024, 3, 1)); Ok(()) }

Generally speaking, whenever there is an operation involving a Span, there is an equivalent operation available with SignedDuration:

use jiff::{civil::date, SignedDuration}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let dt1 = date(2024, 2, 1).at(17, 30, 0, 0); let sdur = SignedDuration::from_mins(90); assert_eq!(dt1.checked_add(sdur)?, date(2024, 2, 1).at(19, 0, 0, 0)); Ok(()) }

Notice that in the above example, we actually switched from using a civil::Date to a civil::DateTime. This was done to show how physical time units can be added. But note that the same can be accomplished with a Span, because it combines all units:

use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let dt1 = date(2024, 2, 1).at(17, 30, 0, 0); let span = 1.hour().minutes(30); assert_eq!(dt1.checked_add(span)?, date(2024, 2, 1).at(19, 0, 0, 0)); // Calendar and physical time units can // be combined! let span = 1.month().hours(1).minutes(30); assert_eq!(dt1.checked_add(span)?, date(2024, 3, 1).at(19, 0, 0, 0)); Ok(()) }

In brief, use a Span when you can. But when it’s too bulky or too slow, use a SignedDuration. One of the key benefits of a Span is that since it represents each unit value distinctly, one can preserve the original meaning of a duration. For example, it’s common to represent the runtime of films in minutes, even when the duration exceeds one hour. Indeed, a span of 2 hours is a distinct span from a span of 120 minutes:

use jiff::ToSpan; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span1 = 2.hours(); let span2 = 120.minutes(); // This means the spans are distinct values // in memory. assert_ne!(span1.fieldwise(), span2.fieldwise()); Ok(()) }

The Span::fieldwise routine converts a Span into a value whose units can be compared in a field-by-field fashion. To compare spans based on the actual physical duration they represent, use Span::compare:

let span1 = 2.hours(); let span2 = 120.minutes(); assert!(span1.compare(span2)?.is_eq());

This was a very brief introduction to durations in Jiff. They are a lot more powerful than what is shown here. You might even try playing with the examples above to explore its nooks and crannies. We’ll cover their API in more detail in a later section.

When should I use Jiff?

Jiff isn’t always the right thing to use. Sometimes you can get by with something simpler.

First and foremost, if you’re measuring the time something takes in a program, you should almost certainly be using monotonic time. This is available via std::time::Instant:

use std::time::{Duration, Instant}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let start = Instant::now(); // do some serious work std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1)); let elapsed = Instant::now().duration_since(start); println!("{elapsed:?}"); Ok(()) }

If you do need to compute elapsed time using your system clock, then Jiff is very convenient for that:

use std::time::Duration; use jiff::Timestamp; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { // assume `start` came from somewhere // over a network let start = Timestamp::now(); std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1)); let elapsed = Timestamp::now().duration_since(start); println!("{elapsed}"); Ok(()) }

But you don’t actually need Jiff for this. A std::time::SystemTime will work perfectly fine:

use std::time::{Duration, SystemTime}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { // assume `start` came from somewhere // over a network let start = SystemTime::now(); std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1)); let elapsed = SystemTime::now().duration_since(start)?; println!("{elapsed:?}"); Ok(()) }

Where Jiff starts to become useful is when you need something beyond just an integer number of seconds since the Unix epoch. For example, some very hairy math is required in order to convert a SystemTime into an RFC 3339 timestamp like 2026-11-14T21:34:00Z.

As long as you can live in UTC completely, don’t care about local time and can work with Unix timestamps only, then the Rust standard library won’t steer you wrong.

Parsing and Formatting

Conversion to and from strings is a major part of Jiff. Jiff’s focus is primarily on interoperability via the following:

RFC 3339 specifies a format for fixed offset instants in time, in terms of a human readable civil datetime. For example, 2026-11-12T15:36:00-05:00. This is the serialization format used by Timestamp. RFC 9557 extends and updates RFC 3339 to add time zone information. For example, 2026-11-12T15:36:00-05:00[America/New_York]. This is the serialization format used by ZonedDateTime. ISO 8601 covers mostly everything else, including durations and civil datetimes. For example, P5Y3MT20H is an ISO 8601 duration and 2026-11-12T15:30:00 is an ISO 8601 civil datetime whose corresponding instant in time is unknown.

What Jiff actually implements is the Temporal RFC 9557 / ISO 8601 grammar for flexible parsing of datetimes from strings. For most use cases, it suffices to think in terms of RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601. But Jiff does support parsing strings that aren’t valid in any of those three specifications. For example, 2026-11-12[America/New_York] parses as if it was 2026-11-12T00:00:00[America/New_York].

In this section, we’ll take a tour of how Jiff does datetime formatting and printing.

FromStr and Display

Every datetime and duration type in Jiff implements the standard library FromStr and Display traits. This means that it’s natural to parse datetimes:

let ts: Timestamp = "2026-10-31T05:15:00Z".parse()?;

and print them:

println!("{ts}");

Parsing is flexible, so even if there are components missing, parsing still succeeds. For example, without minutes or seconds, those components default to zero:

let dt: civil::DateTime = "2026-10-31T05".parse()?; assert_eq!(dt.to_string(), "2026-10-31T05:00:00");

Another example of flexible parsing is that if a string contains another date type, then one can parse that. For example, one can parse a date out of an ISO 8601 datetime:

let d: civil::Date = "2026-10-31T05:30".parse()?; assert_eq!(d.to_string(), "2026-10-31");

A ZonedDateTime always uses RFC 9557 syntax, which includes the IANA time zone identifier:

let zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2026-10-31T05:30[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?; // While the string we parsed didn't have any offset, // one was automatically added by consulting the time // zone definition for the civil datetime provided. assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-10-31T05:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]");

If you want to print a zoned datetime using only RFC 3339 syntax, then you can do so by formatting the timestamp directly with the zoned datetime’s offset:

let zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2026-10-31T05:30[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?; assert_eq!( zdt.timestamp().display_with_offset(zdt.offset()).to_string(), "2026-10-31T05:30:00+11:00", );

The Span and SignedDuration types also support the FromStr and Display traits via the ISO 8601 duration format. For example:

use jiff::{SignedDuration, Span}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let duration = "PT5H30M"; let span: Span = duration.parse()?; assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "PT5H30M"); let sdur: SignedDuration = duration.parse()?; assert_eq!(sdur.to_string(), "PT5H30M"); Ok(()) }

Since a Span is a hybrid duration that also supports calendar units, it can parse durations with calendar units and physical time units. A SignedDuration can only parse durations with physical time units:

use jiff::{SignedDuration, Span}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let duration = "P11Y2M28DT5H30M"; let span: Span = duration.parse()?; assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "P11Y2M28DT5H30M"); let err = duration.parse::<SignedDuration>().unwrap_err(); assert_eq!( err.to_string(), "parsing ISO 8601 duration in this context requires \ that the duration contain a time component \ and no components of days or greater", ); Ok(()) }

The ISO 8601 duration format does, however, have some shortcomings that we’ll discuss in the next section.

The “friendly” Duration Format

Because ISO 8601 duration strings enjoy broad support, it is the default in Jiff for both Span and SignedDuration. However, it has two important shortcomings:

It is difficult to read. For example, in P11Y2M28DT5H30M, the lack of whitespace makes the unit values and the unit labels all run together. An ISO 8601 duration cannot unambiguously represent all possible Span values.

The second shortcoming is best seen with an example. Consider a Span that is 2000 milliseconds. If you convert this to an ISO 8601 duration string and then parse it back, you end up with 2 seconds instead:

use jiff::{Span, ToSpan}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let original = 2000.milliseconds(); assert_eq!(original.to_string(), "PT2S"); let got: Span = "PT2S".parse()?; // The spans have different unit values! assert_eq!(original.get_seconds(), 0); assert_eq!(original.get_milliseconds(), 2000); assert_eq!(got.get_seconds(), 2); assert_eq!(got.get_milliseconds(), 0); Ok(()) }

This might not be desirable for cases where you want a span’s string format to faithfully represent all possible distinct values of a span.

For these two reasons, Jiff comes with its own bespoke “friendly” duration format. The friendly format is non-lossy and is meant to be easier to read for English speakers than the ISO 8601 duration format. Here are some examples that are all valid friendly durations:

40d 40 days 1y1d 1yr 1d 3d4h59m 3 days, 4 hours, 59 minutes 3d 4h 59m 2h30m 2h 30m 1mo 1w 1 week 1w4d 1 wk 4 days 1m 0.0021s 0s 0d 0 days 3 mins 34s 123ms 3 mins 34.123 secs 3 mins 34,123s 1y1mo1d1h1m1.1s 1yr 1mo 1day 1hr 1min 1.1sec 1 year, 1 month, 1 day, 1 hour, 1 minute 1.1 seconds 1 year, 1 month, 1 day, 01:01:01.1

Parsing a friendly duration is as easy as parsing an ISO 8601 duration: the FromStr implementations on both Span and SignedDuration support ISO 8601 durations and friendly durations simultaneously:

let span: Span = "6y 10mo 3d 23h".parse()?; // Recall that `Span::fieldwise` permits // equality comparisons on `Span` in a // unit-by-unit fashion. assert_eq!(span.fieldwise(), 6.years().months(10).days(3).hours(23));

Printing a friendly duration does require a bit more effort, since it isn’t the default. Instead of Span::to_string(), one can use the “alternative” syntax via Rust’s formatting machinery:

let span = 2000.milliseconds(); // This also demonstrates that our unit // values are preserved. assert_eq!(format!("{span:#}"), "2000ms");

One can also use a lower level friendly printer to customize its output. For example, here’s how to write a span in the friendly format to an existing String using more spacing, longer unit labels and commas separating each unit:

use jiff::{fmt::friendly, ToSpan}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { static PRINTER: friendly::SpanPrinter = friendly::SpanPrinter::new() .comma_after_designator(true) .spacing(friendly::Spacing::BetweenUnitsAndDesignators) .designator(friendly::Designator::Verbose); let span = 6.years().months(10).days(3).hours(23); let mut buf = String::new(); PRINTER.print_span(&span, &mut buf)?; assert_eq!(buf, "6 years, 10 months, 3 days, 23 hours"); Ok(()) }

See the jiff::fmt::friendly module for a lot more detail, including a grammar that precisely specifies the format supported.

strptime and strftime

The POSIX strptime and POSIX strftime routines are far from the ideal way to format and parse datetimes, but they are ubiquitous and most programmers are familiar with them. Because of their ubiquity, and because of the utility of being able to format and parse bespoke datetime formats, Jiff provides implementations of these routines that are mostly POSIX compatible.

Every datetime type in Jiff comes with strptime and strftime routines. For example, to parse a civil date in the US month/day/year format:

let date = civil::Date::strptime("%m/%d/%Y", "11/13/2026")?; assert_eq!(date.to_string(), "2026-11-13");

Or to format a zoned datetime in a convenient to read representation for English speakers:

let zdt = civil::date(2026, 11, 13).at(17, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("Australia/Sydney")?; assert_eq!( zdt.strftime("%a, %b %d, %Y %H:%M %Z").to_string(), "Fri, Nov 13, 2026 17:30 AEDT", );

Callers can also use lower level APIs from jiff::fmt::strtime to get access to each parsed component individually:

use jiff::{civil, fmt::strtime::BrokenDownTime}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let tm = BrokenDownTime::parse( "%a, %b %d, %Y %H:%M", "Fri, Nov 13, 2026 17:30", )?; assert_eq!(tm.weekday(), Some(civil::Weekday::Friday)); assert_eq!(tm.month(), Some(11)); assert_eq!(tm.day(), Some(13)); assert_eq!(tm.year(), Some(2026)); assert_eq!(tm.hour(), Some(17)); assert_eq!(tm.minute(), Some(30)); assert_eq!(tm.second(), None); Ok(()) } The jiff::fmt module

While the above tour should cover most use cases, there are sometimes reasons for exerting more control over parsing or formatting. Or for supporting alternate formats like RFC 2822. The jiff::fmt module is meant to cover these use cases at the cost of more complex APIs. For example, consider parsing an RFC 2822 datetime string from a &[u8] (which lets callers avoid a UTF-8 validation check):

use jiff::fmt::rfc2822; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { static PARSER: rfc2822::DateTimeParser = rfc2822::DateTimeParser::new(); let data = b"Sat, 13 Jul 2024 15:09:59 -0400"; let ts = PARSER.parse_timestamp(data)?; assert_eq!(ts.to_string(), "2024-07-13T19:09:59Z"); Ok(()) }

Another example shows how to change the default disambiguation strategy when the provided civil datetime is ambiguous. For example, Sydney, Australia moved the clocks backwards at 2026-04-05T03:00:00 local time. That is, they went from UTC offset +11 to UTC offset +10. So what happens if we try to parse a time on the clock that is repeated as a result?

use jiff::ZonedDateTime; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?; assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]"); Ok(()) }

Here, the first occurrence of 02:30 is selected, just before Sydney leaves daylight saving time. Now, the data itself can actually select the desired offset:

use jiff::ZonedDateTime; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2026-04-05T02:30+11:00[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?; assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]"); let zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2026-04-05T02:30+10:00[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?; assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+10:00[Australia/Sydney]"); Ok(()) }

But this happens because there is no ambiguity in the data. Since the offset is supplied, the exact instant in time is known. Going back to 2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney], which is ambiguous because it could refer to two different instants in time, how do we modify the strategy for resolving that ambiguity? We can’t using the standard library FromStr trait, so we instead have to construct our own parser manually, just like we did for RFC 2822 parsing above. This example shows how to do that and all of the different disambiguation options. Remember, UTC offset +11:00 corresponds to the first occurrence of 2026-04-05T02:30 on the clocks of folks in Sydney while UTC offset +10:00 corresponds to the second occurrence.

use jiff::{fmt::temporal::DateTimeParser, tz::Disambiguation}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let string = "2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney]"; // "compatible" is the default strategy, which selects // the earlier time in a fold (usually moving from daylight // saving time to standard time) and the later time in a // gap (usually moving from standard time to daylight // saving time). let parser = DateTimeParser::new().disambiguation(Disambiguation::Compatible); let zdt = parser.parse_zoned_datetime(string)?; assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]"); // "earlier" always selects the first occurrence // in a fold, or the time before a gap. // So this is the same as compatible in this case, // since our civil time is in a fold. let parser = DateTimeParser::new().disambiguation(Disambiguation::Earlier); let zdt = parser.parse_zoned_datetime(string)?; assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]"); // "later" always selects the second occurrence // in a fold, or the time after a gap. // So this is different from "compatible" for a // fold. Notice that the UTC +10:00 offset is // chosen. let parser = DateTimeParser::new().disambiguation(Disambiguation::Later); let zdt = parser.parse_zoned_datetime(string)?; assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+10:00[Australia/Sydney]"); // "reject" means that if the instant is ambiguous, // then an error is returned. let parser = DateTimeParser::new().disambiguation(Disambiguation::Reject); let err = parser.parse_zoned_datetime(string).unwrap_err(); assert_eq!( err.to_string(), "error converting datetime to instant \ in time zone Australia/Sydney: \ datetime is ambiguous since it falls \ into a fold between offsets +11 and +10", ); Ok(()) }

The jiff::fmt module contains lots of other goodies that we won’t cover here, including, but not limited to:

The ability to format directly into an existing allocation. Parsing a datetime into its individual components. Helpers for serde integration. Locale Sensitive Formatting via ICU4X Integration

No section on datetime formatting would be complete without addressing locales. In this context, a locale is a set of user preferences used for formatting datetimes. This is useful when you want to present a datetime to an end user that doesn’t expect standard formats from RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601.

Jiff itself does not provide any facilities for dealing with locales. Instead, users can opt into this support via the ICU4X project. To make conversions between Jiff and ICU4X, the jiff-icu integration crate can be used.

Here’s an example showing how to format a zoned datetime in the fr-LA locale: (You’ll need to run cargo add icu jiff-icu to your project for this to work.)

use icu::{ calendar::Iso, datetime::{fieldsets, DateTimeFormatter}, locale::locale, time::{zone::models::AtTime, TimeZoneInfo}, }; use jiff::ZonedDateTime; use jiff_icu::ConvertFrom as _; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { // Firstly, do a conversion from Jiff's zoned datetime to ICU's. let jiff_zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2024-09-10T23:37:20-04[America/New_York]".parse()?; let icu_zdt = icu::time::ZonedDateTime::<Iso, TimeZoneInfo<AtTime>>::convert_from( &jiff_zdt, ); // Second, create a datetime formatter for the fr-LA locale: let formatter = DateTimeFormatter::try_new( locale!("fr-LA").into(), fieldsets::YMDET::medium().with_zone(fieldsets::zone::SpecificLong), )?; // Thirdly, format the zoned datetime. assert_eq!( formatter.format(&icu_zdt).to_string(), "mar. 10 sept. 2024, 23:37:20 heure d’été de l’Est nord-américain", ); Ok(()) }

The ICU4X API has a lot of options for customizing datetime formatting. Exploring it further is outside the scope of this blog.

Date Manipulation

Jiff provides many methods on its datetime types to make using them as comfortable and error-free as possible.

Date Basics

Every datetime type provides a new constructor that lets callers build it from its constituent parts. In most cases, this constructor is fallible. For example:

use jiff::civil::Date; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let d = Date::new(2024, 2, 29)?; // All datetime types have convenient // accessors for each of their components. assert_eq!(d.year(), 2024); assert_eq!(d.month(), 2); assert_eq!(d.day(), 29); let err = Date::new(2025, 2, 29).unwrap_err(); assert_eq!( err.to_string(), "parameter 'day' for `2025-02` is invalid, must be in range `1..=28`", ); Ok(()) }

Because creating dates is so common, there is a shorthand for doing so when you know the inputs are valid:

let d = const { civil::date(2024, 2, 29) }; assert_eq!(d.year(), 2024); assert_eq!(d.month(), 2); assert_eq!(d.day(), 29);

That is, civil::date is a const function that will panic if its inputs are invalid. It should only be used with inputs that are known to be valid. It would, for example, be inappropriate to use this with user provided values. Because of the const block above, if you try to provide invalid values, you’ll get a compiler error.

For datetime types that represent an instant in time (i.e., ZonedDateTime and Timestamp), there is also a now() constructor for getting the current time:

use jiff::{Timestamp, ZonedDateTime}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let now = Timestamp::now(); println!("{now}"); // Example output: 2026-11-15T14:17:21.80099287Z // This will automatically fetch your system's configured time zone. let now = ZonedDateTime::now(); println!("{now}"); // Example output: 2026-11-15T09:17:21.80102125-05:00[America/New_York] Ok(()) }

In addition to constructors, new date values can be constructed from old date values using the Date::with API:

let d1 = const { civil::date(2024, 2, 29) }; // This API doesn't break just because 31 // is supplied before a month that has 31 // days. Any order is fine! This is because // errors are deferred until `build()` is // called. let d2 = d1.with().day(31).month(3).build()?; assert_eq!(d2.to_string(), "2024-03-31");

Once you have a date, there are oodles of APIs available:

let d = civil::date(2025, 7, 10); assert_eq!(d.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Thursday); assert_eq!(d.first_of_year(), civil::date(2025, 1, 1)); assert_eq!(d.last_of_year(), civil::date(2025, 12, 31)); assert_eq!(d.first_of_month(), civil::date(2025, 7, 1)); assert_eq!(d.last_of_month(), civil::date(2025, 7, 31)); assert_eq!(d.yesterday()?, civil::date(2025, 7, 9)); assert_eq!(d.tomorrow()?, civil::date(2025, 7, 11));

Moreover, because of the datetime onion, all of these APIs are also available on civil::DateTime and ZonedDateTime:

let create_zdt = |date: civil::Date| -> Result<ZonedDateTime, jiff::Error> { date.at(0, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York") }; let zdt = create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 10))?; assert_eq!(zdt.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Thursday); assert_eq!(zdt.first_of_year()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 1, 1))?); assert_eq!(zdt.last_of_year()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 12, 31))?); assert_eq!(zdt.first_of_month()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 1))?); assert_eq!(zdt.last_of_month()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 31))?); assert_eq!(zdt.yesterday()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 9))?); assert_eq!(zdt.tomorrow()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 11))?);

These routines on ZonedDateTime also take time zone transitions into account. For example, ZonedDateTime knows that tomorrow() doesn’t always add 24 hours:

// On 2024-11-03 at 2AM in New York, time was rolled // back 1 hour in the transition from daylight saving // time to standard time. That means 2024-11-03 was // actually 25 hours long in New York. let zdt = civil::date(2024, 11, 2).at(17, 25, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let tomorrow = zdt.tomorrow()?; assert_eq!(tomorrow.datetime(), civil::date(2024, 11, 3).at(17, 25, 0, 0)); // The physical time difference between them is 25 hours! let span = tomorrow - zdt; assert_eq!(format!("{span:#}"), "25h");

NOTE: We’ll talk about date arithmetic in the next section.

When ZonedDateTime::tomorrow() (among other APIs that produce a ZonedDateTime) would land in a gap or a fold, the “compatible” disambiguation strategy is chosen automatically:

// For a zoned datetime that lands // in a fold, the earlier instant is // chosen by default. let zdt = civil::date(2024, 11, 2).at(1, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let tomorrow = zdt.tomorrow()?; assert_eq!( tomorrow.to_string(), "2024-11-03T01:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]" ); // And for a gap, the later instant // is chosen by default. let zdt = civil::date(2024, 3, 9).at(2, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let tomorrow = zdt.tomorrow()?; assert_eq!( tomorrow.to_string(), "2024-03-10T03:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]" );

To override this behavior, you can drop down to civil datetimes, perform the operation, and then use TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime to control the exact disambiguation strategy:

// For a zoned datetime that lands // in a fold, the earlier instant is // chosen by default. But let's say // we want the later instant. let zdt = civil::date(2024, 11, 2).at(1, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let tomorrow = zdt .time_zone() .to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(zdt.datetime().tomorrow()?) .later()?; assert_eq!( tomorrow.to_string(), // Notice that the offset is now -05, // which corresponds to the later // instant. "2024-11-03T01:30:00-05:00[America/New_York]" );

There are a few other methods of note on date types that are worth mentioning. First is the ability to query for things like, “The Thursday after next” or “The last Sunday of the month.” The former can be answered by the nth_weekday API:

let zdt1 = civil::date(2024, 7, 10).in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!(zdt1.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Wednesday); // Not this Thursday, but the next! let zdt2 = zdt1.nth_weekday(2, civil::Weekday::Thursday)?; assert_eq!(zdt2.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Thursday); assert_eq!(zdt2.date(), civil::date(2024, 7, 18));

While the latter can be answered by the nth_weekday_of_month API:

let zdt1 = civil::date(2024, 7, 10).in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!(zdt1.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Wednesday); // The last Sunday of this month. let zdt2 = zdt1.nth_weekday_of_month(-1, civil::Weekday::Sunday)?; assert_eq!(zdt2.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Sunday); assert_eq!(zdt2.date(), civil::date(2024, 7, 28));

Finally, users can access a convenient time series iterator via series:

use jiff::{civil, ToSpan}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let start = civil::date(2024, 7, 10).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let mut dates = vec![]; // Every week for 8 weeks. for zdt in start.series(1.week()).take(8) { dates.push(zdt); } assert_eq!( dates, vec![ civil::date(2024, 7, 10).in_tz("America/New_York")?, civil::date(2024, 7, 17).in_tz("America/New_York")?, civil::date(2024, 7, 24).in_tz("America/New_York")?, civil::date(2024, 7, 31).in_tz("America/New_York")?, civil::date(2024, 8, 7).in_tz("America/New_York")?, civil::date(2024, 8, 14).in_tz("America/New_York")?, civil::date(2024, 8, 21).in_tz("America/New_York")?, civil::date(2024, 8, 28).in_tz("America/New_York")?, ] ); Ok(()) }

All of these methods are also available on civil::Date and civil::DateTime, which should make it very natural to move between them.

Date Arithmetic

All datetime types in Jiff support adding and subtracting durations, and finding the span of time between two datetime values. Let’s start with a civil::Date:

use jiff::{civil, ToSpan}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let d1 = civil::date(2024, 7, 30); let d2 = d1 + 2.days(); assert_eq!(d2, civil::date(2024, 8, 1)); Ok(()) }

Here we make use of the std::ops::Add trait implementation for civil::Date. The downside of using this, though, is that if the date value goes out of range, then it panics. That may or may not be acceptable. But if you’re dealing with user inputs, then you should use Date::checked_add instead:

use jiff::{civil, ToSpan}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let d1 = civil::date(2024, 7, 30); let d2 = d1.checked_add(2.days())?; assert_eq!(d2, civil::date(2024, 8, 1)); Ok(()) }

Let’s take a look at a few other examples involving months and years:

let d = civil::date(2024, 5, 31); assert_eq!(d.checked_add(1.month())?, civil::date(2024, 6, 30)); assert_eq!(d.checked_add(2.months())?, civil::date(2024, 7, 31)); let d = civil::date(2025, 1, 31); assert_eq!(d.checked_add(1.month())?, civil::date(2025, 2, 28)); let d = civil::date(2024, 2, 29); let span = 1.year().months(2).days(5); assert_eq!(d.checked_add(span)?, civil::date(2025, 5, 4));

As with other methods on Date, they are also available on ZonedDateTime:

let d = civil::date(2024, 5, 31).at(13, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!( d.checked_add(1.month())?, civil::date(2024, 6, 30).at(13, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")? );

If we take a look at the type signature for ZonedDateTime::checked_add, we can see that it’s actually polymorphic:

pub fn checked_add<A: Into<ZonedDateTimeArithmetic>>( &self, duration: A, ) -> Result<ZonedDateTime, Error>

Specifically, it accepts anything that can be converted into a ZonedDateTimeArithmetic. In this case, there are From trait implementations for the following types:

This means that ZonedDateTime::checked_add can accept any one of these duration values:

use jiff::{civil, SignedDuration}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let d = civil::date(2024, 5, 31).at(13, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!( d.checked_add(SignedDuration::from_mins(45))?, civil::date(2024, 5, 31).at(14, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")? ); Ok(()) }

This type of polymorphism is common in Jiff. Here, it is merely used to provide a convenient way to use multiple duration types. But as we’ll see, it’s also used to provide an extension point for configuration options that control how the operation works.

In addition to adding or subtracting durations from datetime values, one can also compute the duration between two datetime values. For example, to get the number of days between two dates:

use jiff::{civil, ToSpan}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let d1 = civil::date(2024, 5, 31); let d2 = civil::date(2024, 9, 30); assert_eq!(d2 - d1, 122.days().fieldwise()); Ok(()) }

Similarly, we can use Date::until to compute the span between dates:

let d1 = civil::date(2024, 5, 31); let d2 = civil::date(2024, 9, 30); assert_eq!(d1.until(d2)?, 122.days().fieldwise());

Like with Date::checked_add, this routine is also available at ZonedDateTime::until:

let zdt1 = civil::date(2024, 5, 31).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let zdt2 = civil::date(2024, 9, 30).in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!(zdt1.until(&zdt2)?, 2928.hours().fieldwise());

Notice though that hours, instead of days, are returned. This is because two ZonedDateTime values might be in different time zones. Since a ZonedDateTime is fundamentally an instant in time, and because days might be of varying length depending on the time zone, defaulting to hours as the largest possible unit means subtracting two zoned datetimes will always succeed. However, we can request larger units in the duration returned by passing additional options. Notably, ZonedDateTime::until is polymorphic:

pub fn until<'a, A: Into<ZonedDateTimeDifference<'a>>>( &self, other: A, ) -> Result<Span, Error>

That is, callers aren’t just limited to passing a ZonedDateTime here, but anything that can be converted to a ZonedDateTimeDifference. Here is one such example, where we can override the largest units returned in the duration:

use jiff::{civil, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let zdt1 = civil::date(2024, 5, 31).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let zdt2 = civil::date(2024, 9, 30).in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!( zdt1.until((Unit::Month, &zdt2))?, 3.months().days(30).fieldwise() ); Ok(()) }

A ZonedDateTimeDifference provides much more powerful configuration options for rounding the span returned. Take this example, which produces a span with many unit values:

use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let zdt1 = date(2024, 5, 15).at(14, 30, 54, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let zdt2 = date(2024, 5, 31) .at(19, 13, 27, 123_456_789) .in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!( zdt1.until((Unit::Day, &zdt2))?, 16.days() .hours(4) .minutes(42) .seconds(33) .milliseconds(123) .microseconds(456) .nanoseconds(789) .fieldwise(), ); Ok(()) }

This might be too much precision to show to an end user. Instead, perhaps we’d like to round the span to the nearest half-hour. We can do this by building a ZonedDateTimeDifference explicitly and configuring its options:

use jiff::{civil::date, RoundMode, ToSpan, Unit, ZonedDateTimeDifference}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let zdt1 = date(2024, 5, 15).at(14, 30, 54, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let zdt2 = date(2024, 5, 31) .at(19, 13, 27, 123_456_789) .in_tz("America/New_York")?; let difference = ZonedDateTimeDifference::new(&zdt2) .largest(Unit::Day) .smallest(Unit::Minute) .increment(30) .mode(RoundMode::HalfExpand); assert_eq!( zdt1.until(difference)?, 16.days().hours(4).minutes(30).fieldwise(), ); Ok(()) }

Note also that rounding a span takes time zone transitions like daylight saving time into account. For example, let’s take 2024-11-02 17:30 and 2024-11-03 04:45 in New York. Because New York stopped daylight saving time at 2AM on 2024-11-03, the amount of physical time between them is 12 hours and 15 minutes:

let zdt1 = date(2024, 11, 2).at(17, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let zdt2 = date(2024, 11, 3).at(4, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!(zdt2 - zdt1, 12.hours().minutes(15).fieldwise());

Normally, if we rounded to the nearest day, this would round up to 1 day. But since the midpoint of this particular day is actually 12 hours and 30 minutes, this duration will round down to 0 days when we request it:

use jiff::{civil::date, RoundMode, ToSpan, Unit, ZonedDateTimeDifference}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let zdt1 = date(2024, 11, 2).at(17, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let zdt2 = date(2024, 11, 3).at(4, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?; let difference = ZonedDateTimeDifference::new(&zdt2) .largest(Unit::Day) .smallest(Unit::Day) .mode(RoundMode::HalfExpand); assert_eq!(zdt1.until(difference)?, 0.days().fieldwise()); Ok(()) }

Next we’ll continue our discussion of rounding, but when applied to datetimes themselves.

Date Rounding

Date rounding in Jiff is limited to units of days or lower. Therefore, it’s only available on ZonedDateTime, Timestamp, civil::DateTime, civil::Time but not civil::Date.

A common example for rounding a datetime is to reduce precision. For example, a system clock might provide nanosecond precision, but maybe we only care about the nearest half-hour:

use jiff::{civil::date, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let zdt = date(2024, 11, 2) .at(17, 46, 20, 123_456_789) .in_tz("America/New_York")?; assert_eq!( zdt.to_string(), "2024-11-02T17:46:20.123456789-04:00[America/New_York]" ); // Round to the nearest half hour. let rounded = zdt.round((Unit::Minute, 30))?; assert_eq!( rounded.to_string(), "2024-11-02T18:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]" ); Ok(()) }

As with rounding spans, rounding a ZonedDateTime is aware of time zone transitions:

let zdt = date(2024, 11, 3) .at(11, 45, 20, 123_456_789) .in_tz("America/New_York")?; // Round to the nearest day. let rounded = zdt.round(Unit::Day)?; assert_eq!( rounded.to_string(), "2024-11-04T00:00:00-05:00[America/New_York]" );

Notice that in the above example, our time of 11:45AM is before noon, yet the result still rounds up to the next day. This is because the midpoint for this day is 11:30AM since, by 11:30AM, 12.5 hours have already elapsed because of the repeated 1AM hour in the move away from daylight saving time in New York.

Other Calendars

Jiff itself doesn’t support any calendars other than the proleptic Gregorian calendar. One can instead use the ICU4X crate to work in non-Gregorian calendars, and convert between datetime types using the jiff-icu crate: (Use cargo add icu jiff-icu to make this example work.)

use icu::{ calendar::{types::Month, Date as IcuDate}, time::{DateTime as IcuDateTime, Time as IcuTime}, }; use jiff::civil::DateTime; use jiff_icu::ConvertTryFrom as _; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { // Firstly, create an ICU datetime using the Hebrew calendar. let datetime = IcuDateTime { date: IcuDate::try_new_hebrew_v2(5785, Month::new(5), 4)?, time: IcuTime::try_new(17, 30, 0, 0)?, }; // Secondly, convert it to a civil datetime. // This will automatically use ICU to convert // the date from the Hebrew calendar to the // Gregorian (or ISO) calendar. let zdt = DateTime::convert_try_from(datetime)?; assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2025-02-02T17:30:00"); Ok(()) }

The ICU4X API supports many more calendars.

Which DateTime Type Do I Use?

There are 3 potentially confusable datetime types in Jiff:

When should you use each one versus the other?

To a first approximation, if you can use a ZonedDateTime, then that is probably the type you want to reach for. It represents a specific instant in time in a particular geographic location. That is, it has both a Timestamp and a TimeZone.

If you only ever need to work in UTC or just deal with system time, then a Timestamp is probably the right choice. This is useful for representing a specific instant in time that is not connected to any time zone.

A civil::DateTime is useful in contexts where you don’t care about a specific instant in time and when calcuations should be done independent of time zone. For example, when parsing datetime information from a user interface datetime picker.

Remember that both a civil::DateTime and a Timestamp can be converted to a ZonedDateTime by supplying a time zone.

Span Manipulation

We’ve already seen how to add spans to datetime values and how to get spans as a difference between datetime values. But we haven’t yet explored the APIs available on a Span itself.

First and foremost, we can build a Span through its constructor, which returns a Span with all of its units set to 0:

use jiff::Span; let span = Span::new();

A Span is both Copy and immutable. We can create new spans through method chaining:

let span = Span::new().hours(1).minutes(30); assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "PT1H30M");

Or we can use the ToSpan convenience trait, which adds methods on integer types for constructing spans:

use jiff::ToSpan; let span = 1.hour().minutes(30); assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "PT1H30M");

Note though that methods like Span::hours and ToSpan::hours will panic when the integer is outside the limits of what Span supports. This is fine when your spans are literals in your program, since a panic would indicate a bug. But if your inputs come from an end user, it’s better to use fallible methods:

let span = Span::new().try_hours(1)?.try_minutes(30)?; assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "PT1H30M");

Spans preserve each individual unit value. This means that 90 minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes, while they represent the same duration, are actually different values in memory:

let span1 = 1.hour().minutes(30); let span2 = 90.minutes(); assert_eq!(span1.to_string(), "PT1H30M"); assert_eq!(span2.to_string(), "PT90M");

This permits callers maximum flexibility when it comes to representing durations. This makes it possible to represent durations in a specific unit even when they add up to larger units. For example, the runtime duration of films is typically conveyed in minutes, even when the runtime exceeds one hour. This can be adjusted programmatically using Span::round:

use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span1 = 1.hour().minutes(30); let span2 = span1.round(SpanRound::new().largest(Unit::Minute))?; assert_eq!(span2.to_string(), "PT90M"); Ok(()) }

You can go the other way as well:

use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span1 = 90.minutes(); let span2 = span1.round(SpanRound::new().largest(Unit::Hour))?; assert_eq!(span2.to_string(), "PT1H30M"); Ok(()) }

Neither of these examples do actual rounding, despite the name of the API. Instead, since we’re only setting the largest unit, this API is doing unit balancing. Unit balancing is when all unit values rollover into larger units up until the largest configured unit. This works even for calendar units too, but you need to provide a relative date:

use jiff::{civil, SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span = 2756.hours(); let dt = civil::date(2020, 1, 1).at(0, 0, 0, 0); let round = SpanRound::new().largest(Unit::Year).relative(dt); assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "3mo 23d 20h"); Ok(()) }

Without a relative date, it’s not possible to know how many hours are in a single month. That is, once calendar units are involved, a span cannot be interpreted as a physical duration of time until some context is applied.

The same even applies to days themselves, since days can sometimes be more or less than 24 hours. Take the above example. What happens if we use a zoned datetime as our relative date instead?

use jiff::{civil, SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span = 2756.hours(); let zdt = civil::date(2020, 1, 1).at(0, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("Europe/Rome")?; let round = SpanRound::new().largest(Unit::Year).relative(&zdt); assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "3mo 23d 21h"); Ok(()) }

Notice that the duration’s hour component changed from 20 to 21. Why? Because we started with 2756 hour in both cases and because 2020-03-29 in Rome was only 23 hours long (in a move from standard time to daylight saving time). That means that one of those days in 3mo 23d was only 23 hours long. So an extra hour needed to be added to make up for it.

The round API can also do actual rounding:

use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span = 2.hours().minutes(30); let round = SpanRound::new().smallest(Unit::Hour); assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "3h"); Ok(()) }

You can also change its rounding mode from the default (“half-expand”, or like you were taught rounding in school) to truncation (or one of several other modes):

use jiff::{RoundMode, SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span = 2.hours().minutes(30); let round = SpanRound::new().smallest(Unit::Hour).mode(RoundMode::Trunc); assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "2h"); Ok(()) }

One can also specify a rounding increment to round to the nearest unit value. For example, to the nearest half-hour:

use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span = 2.hours().minutes(31); let round = SpanRound::new().smallest(Unit::Minute).increment(30); assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "2h 30m"); Ok(()) }

Because a Span value cannot easily be compared correctly based purely on its value in memory, a dedicated comparison Span::compare routine is provided:

let span1 = 2.hours(); let span2 = 120.minutes(); assert!(span1.compare(span2)?.is_eq());

Also, one can convert a Span to a floating point value in terms of any unit. For example:

use jiff::{ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span = 90.minutes(); assert_eq!(span.total(Unit::Hour)?, 1.5); Ok(()) }

Converting to calendar units requires a relative date for the same reasons discussed above:

use jiff::{civil, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span = 24.hours(); assert_eq!( span.total((Unit::Month, civil::date(2026, 6, 1)))?, 0.03333333333333333 ); assert_eq!( span.total((Unit::Month, civil::date(2026, 7, 1)))?, 0.03225806451612903 ); Ok(()) } Conclusion

So far, we’ve explored a good chunk of Jiff’s API. We didn’t talk about every nook and cranny, but I think we’ve covered the most important pieces.

We’ll wrap up by briefly discussing motivation and inspiration.

Motivation

Whenever I needed datetime handling in Rust, I always got confused. Should I use chrono or time? How do I get my local time from a timestamp? How do I use my system’s time zone database? How do I do calendar arithmetic?

Before I started working on Jiff, this confusion got annoying enough for me to consider writing my own crate. I felt like the APIs of both chrono and time could be improved upon. I personally found the domain quite interesting and so set out to build something better.

Why not improve on an existing solution, like chrono or time, instead of adding yet another choice into the ecosystem? I do think there are material downsides of having too many choices, but I had concluded that both chrono and time (in 2024) had reached a local maximum. Moreover, in 2024, I was not an expert in datetime handling. It took building a datetime library to become one. So convincing crate maintainers to go in a radically different direction would have been a tall order.

Jiff’s design and comparison documentation contain much more detail regarding the motivation and specific examples between Jiff, chrono and time.

Inspiration

Jiff is heavily inspired by Temporal, which is JavaScript’s standard library solution for date and time management. Jiff inherits API design, functionality and even parsing/formatting of datetime values. Note though that Jiff is not and does not aim to be a 100% compatible implementation of the Temporal specification. Jiff is meant to be a Rust ecosystem library first and foremost.

With that said, if you’re familiar with Temporal and Rust, then it’s likely you’ll find Jiff to be a relatively straightforward translation of Temporal’s API to Rust. This example shows how to use Temporal to round a calendar span to the nearest number of days relative to a date:

const duration = Temporal.Duration.from({ months: 1, days: 1, hours: 1 }); const roundedDuration = duration.round({ largestUnit: "days", smallestUnit: "days", relativeTo: Temporal.PlainDateTime.from("2022-01-01"), }); console.log(roundedDuration); // "P32D"

And here’s the equivalent operation in Jiff:

use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit}; fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let span = 1.month().days(1).hours(1); let rounded_span = span.round( SpanRound::new() .largest(Unit::Day) .smallest(Unit::Day) .relative("2022-01-01".parse::<jiff::civil::Date>()?), )?; assert_eq!(rounded_span.to_string(), "P32D"); Ok(()) }

The main difference between these examples is that Jiff’s duration type is named Span instead of Duration. This was done to avoid confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Duration type.

Here are some other differences:

Temporal’s Instant type in Jiff is named Timestamp in order to avoid confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Instant type. Temporal’s “plain” date and time types are called “civil” in Jiff. Jiff only supports the Gregorian calendar. Jiff’s datetime range only extends to +/- 9999, whereas Temporal’s range is larger.

It’s easy to say that without Temporal, Jiff wouldn’t exist in its current form today.

Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays
